  • Recent findings suggest that I was walking the edge of a small canyon in Colorado’s San Juan National Forest when a rifle roared half a mile or so ahead of me.
  • Sources indicate that when I heard the shot I decided to get to a vantage point on the plateau as fast as I could, so I took off at a dead run.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, this story, “Greatest Mule Deer of Them All,” appeared in the December 1975 matter of Outdoor Life. Burris’ buck remains, all these years later, the No. 1 typical mule deer buck ever taken by a hunter, according to the Boone and Crockett Club. The antlers are now owned by Cabela’s. Burris tagged the buck on Oct. 19, 1972 in Dolores County, Colorado.

Recent findings suggest that I was walking the edge of a small canyon in Colorado’s San Juan National Forest when a rifle roared half a mile or so ahead of me. Till then I’d figured on stillhunting to a plateau covered with scattered oak brush 400 yards north of me. A clump of brush there would have been a fine place to take a stand.

Sources indicate that when I heard the shot I decided to get to a vantage point on the plateau as fast as I could, so I took off at a dead run. I was almost on the plateau when I noticed movement in the oak brush and aspens on the other side of the canyon. I slammed to a stop and stared at the biggest deer I had ever seen. His body was enormous, and his rack seemed large enough for an elk.

Industry observers note that he wasn’t running flat out, but I knew I had to shoot in a hurry. The range was about 250 yards. The buck was moving up the canyon and away from me when I found him in my Leupold 3X-to-9X scope, I put the crosshairs on his back and touched off my Sako .264. He went down in his tracks. My major-game handloads consist of 125-grain Nosler bullets backed with 66.5 grains of No. 4831 powder. It’s a very potent load.

Recent findings suggest that related: My First Buck Was the Biggest Typical Mule Deer Ever Taken with a Bow. I Almost Discarded the Antlers.

According to recent reports, I watched him for a while to make sure he wasn’t going to get up, and then I ran down a side canyon and up the other side of the significant one to the fallen buck. When I ran my hands over the huge 18-point rack, I knew the antlers were very good. I was sure the deer would score high in the Boone and Crockett Club’s record book.

If someone could have told me that my 1969 Colorado buck wasn’t even good enough to make the minimum score for listing in the record book, I wouldn’t have believed him. That’s the way it turned out, but a still bigger deer was ranging the same stretch of country.

Recent findings suggest that I’m 37. My wife and I live in Seguin, Texas, with our 17-year-old son and two daughters, aged 15 and eight. I’m a construction superintendent with an outfit that builds shopping centers, high-rise office buildings, and similar units.

According to recent reports, except for 3½ years spent in the U.S. Air Force, I’ve lived in Texas all my life. I began hunting when I was seven. My dad got me started and taught me to be a good hunter. I killed my first Texas whitetail when I was 13, and I’ve been nuts about deer hunting ever since. Though many of our Texas deer are so small we call them jackrabbits, we do have some large whitetails in the southern brush country. Some of those bucks field-dress at 200 pounds or a bit more, and some have exceptional antlers. Many years of hunting brush-country deer gave me trophy-hunting fever.

I have always wanted to hunt Dall or Stone sheep in Alaska or British Columbia, but I’ve never had the money or the time. I finally decided that the next-best thing was to stay with deer and hunt trophy antlers.

Recent findings suggest that my interest in camping had a lot to do with that first mule-deer hunt in Colorado in 1969. My friends and I have several four-wheel-drive vehicles and an assortment of camping gear. Charlie Fuller of Floresville, and Jack Smith of San Antonio, do a lot of hunting with me. Jack is my age. He’s a carpenter. Charlie, a few years younger, has a fertilizer-application operation. Both like to hunt deer the way I do, and they like to camp. Early in 1969 we decided to hunt in the mountains where we could camp on public land and do without guides and outfitters. We call it a “poor-boy hunt.”.

I did quite a bit of research on trophy mule deer before we chose the San Juan National Forest. From what I’d read in Outdoor Life and other outdoor magazines, I knew that many giant bucks were taken not too far from the Four Corners, where Utah, Arizona, Fresh Mexico, and Colorado touch.

I also bought a copy of the 1964 edition of the Boone and Crockett Club’s book, Records of North American Major Game. Study of the section on mule-deer trophies backed up my contention that southwestern Colorado would be a good place to go. We knew there were better bets, such as the Jicarilla Apache Reservation in New Mexico, but we couldn’t get permits, and we wanted to go into country where we could camp on public land. We eventually drove to Cortez, Colorado, and hunted northeast of town.

The three of us all got bucks that first year, and my big buck had a rack that measured 41 inches across the outside spread. Each antler had “cheater” points extending horizontally from the outside curves of the main beams. Though the rack had a very unusual spread, the tines weren’t very long, and that’s why my trophy didn’t make the record book.

When I killed the deer, I didn’t know much about official scoring systems for massive game, but I did know that where there was one grandote (a Mexican term we use for big bucks) there should be more. We didn’t need a better reason to head back into the same area. We’ve never been sorry.

The second year, I got a buck with a 33-inch outside spread. The third year, I was lucky enough to come up with another good deer. Every season I’ve hunted in those mountains, except one, I’ve taken a buck with an outside antler spread of 30 inches or better, and other members of my party have taken very good bucks too. Many hunters in the area kill deer with spreads as narrow as 12 inches. Every fall I pass up many deer to get the best one I can find.

Most of the men in our group hunt that way. We all love the mountains, and we like to hunt hard from dawn to dark. We don’t want to miss one minute of hunting on these trips. None of us will take a small buck unless time is running out on the last day.

According to recent reports, I don’t want to imply that we’re trophy crazy. Much of our pleasure derives from the planning and preparation that goes into our hunts and the talkfests that go on for months after each trip. We make the most of camp life too. I’m usually the cook because I enjoy it. We come into camp each evening, warm up by our wood stove in the cooktent, swap stories about what happened during the day, and take our time over meals while we plan the next day’s hunt. Then we sack out early enough for a good rest so that we can do it all over again.

We go back into the Cortez area each year because it has proved itself, and because our camping gear is suited to that kind of country. We’re not equipped to backpack into remote areas or pack in with horses.

Recent findings suggest that our cooktent, which also serves as a community area, is a 14 x 16-foot wall tent. We have 9 x 12 Coleman sleeping tents. Everybody contributes something to our outfit. We found out during our first trip that it’s best to take plenty of blankets and raingear.

On the front end of our trailer is mounted a large box in which we pack all our food and some other items. If the weather is warm during our hunt, we have all our venison butchered, wrapped, and quick-frozen in Cortez. We pack the meat and dry ice in the box for our trip home. If the weather is cold, we hang our field-dressed deer from a game pole and then haul them home whole for butchering there. Either way, the venison we put in our freezers provides delicious meals far into the winter.

Industry observers note that we make our trips from Texas to Colorado with two 4WD’s. The substantial unit is my three-quarter-ton Dodge Power Wagon equipped with a winch. Behind the Dodge we tow a Jeep on a 20-foot trailer. We usually ride in the wagon and pack the Jeep and the trailer with gear.

Recent findings suggest that our average cost per man totals about $155, and that includes Colorado’s nonresident deer license ($50). A big chunk of the rest of each man’s expenses goes for gas. We drive straight through from Texas. That takes 20 to 24 hours, depending on driving conditions. We use the Jeep each day to put men out in hunting areas, so we burn a lot of gas. We bring plenty of steaks and a normal supply of groceries such as beans, potatoes, flour, canned goods, breakfast mixes.

I don’t want to imply that we’re trophy crazy. Much of our pleasure derives from the planning and preparation that goes into our hunts and the talkfests that go on for months after each trip. We make the most of camp life too.

It has been revealed that we plan to arrive in our hunting area the Thursday before the Saturday opener of the deer season, which is always in late October. It takes two days to set up camp, get organized, and do a little scouting. We figure on hunting three to five days, but we do not set up a hard-and-fast schedule.

As few as two men have gone to Colorado with me and as many as eight, but everything seems to go along smoothest with about four in the party. In 1972, the year I shot the world-record mule deer, there were four of us. Jack Smith went along, but Charlie Fuller couldn’t get away. Robbie Roe and Bruce Winters were my other partners. I knew them through my job, and we had done a lot of hunting together.

According to recent reports, we drove up into Colorado and camped in the same spot I’d picked out four years earlier. I knew the hunting country fairly well by that time, and I had selected five specific areas that seemed to hold the most deer and the biggest bucks. They’re all laced with relatively thick oak brush, some aspens, and a few pines. Thick oak brush is the key to success. If you’ve got tangles of that stuff and lots of them, you’re going to find deer.

In a recent development, the oak-brush areas most attractive to deer run to broken terrain in the form of canyons and side canyons, plateaus, and mesas. The best technique for hunting that kind of terrain is a combination of stillhunting and standing. I like to stillhunt the plateaus and small canyons. I’ve learned that deer work the small finger canyons and get down into the very bottoms of them. They range back and forth through the canyons, often go up on the mesas and plateaus.

In a recent development, that’s why the combination of hunting techniques works so well. When I’m stillhunting I often spot deer ahead of me or across a canyon or draw. If I take a stand on a good vantage point I may have deer working toward me.

It has been revealed that the problem is that deer may use one area today and vacate it tomorrow. So I choose an area and hunt it out. If deer are there, I stick with it; if they aren’t I move to the next area. That isn’t hard to do, because the San Juan country is mostly rolling terrain, and the altitude is only about 8,500 feet where we hunt.

Our first day of hunting in 1972 began in typical fashion. We checked the wind direction before dawn and decided on the areas each man would hunt. Then we piled into the Jeep and headed up a mountain two-track. I dropped Robbie off first and then Bruce. A few miles farther on, Jack got out of the vehicle. Dawn wasn’t much more than a dull-gray promise in the eastern sky. The black void above us was spitting drizzle.

According to recent reports, “Robbie and Bruce will walk back to camp whenever they feel like it,” I told Jack. “You want me to pick you up at a set time, or do you want to hunt all day in the rain?”.

“I’ll meet you right here at dark,” Jack answered.

I knew he’d say something like that. Jack likes to hunt as much as I do.

We all saw many deer that day, but all the bucks were small. None of us fired a shot.

Industry observers note that but I came very close to filling my tag on the second day of the hunt. It drizzled again, and I just ambled along till 10 o’clock. Then I got real serious about my stillhunting. I don’t know why, but the really big bucks in that area seem to move mostly from 10 in the morning till about 1 in the afternoon.

About noon I spotted a deer in thick oak brush 200 yards ahead. We were both on a plateau. The animal was a substantial one, so I assumed he was a buck, and I started moving in on him. My stalking was quiet because everything was wet, but I couldn’t close the distance very fast in that thick brush, and the deer kept moving away from me as he browsed.

According to recent reports, at one point I saw part of his rack, just enough to know the antlers were in the trophy class. The excitement ended when I tried to cut him off at the edge of the plateau. When I got there, he was gone. I’ll never know whether that buck sensed my presence or went off on a predetermined course.

It has been revealed that when Jack and I got back to camp two bucks were on the game pole. Robbie had nailed a five-pointer with his 7-mm. Remington Magnum rifle equipped with a Leupold scope. Bruce’s deer was also a five-pointer, but the antlers were heavier. Bruce collected his venison with a Winchester Model 70 .30/06 rigged with a Leupold scope.

Sources indicate that when we awoke the third morning, the dad-gummed drizzle was still with us. I suited up in my Browning raingear and filled my pockets with dried fruits and jerky. I knew it would be another long day before I could bake myself beside the wood stove in the cooktent. I dropped Jack off on the trail and then drove on and parked near the area I had hunted the day before.

A slight breeze was coming down off the mountain, so I decided to stillhunt into it and get farther back into rougher country. About 9 o’clock I started into a 400-yard-wide canyon and began working up toward one rim. I was about three-quarters of the way to the top when I spotted two bucks feeding in a clearing 1,000 yards away in the canyon. I stopped and watched them for several minutes because I was astonished that I could see their racks from such a great distance with the naked eye.

Then I looked at them through my Bausch & Lomb 7 x 35 binoculars. Both were definitely in the trophy class. It was fairly late in our hunt, so I decided it was best to cash in on one of them. I’d make the stalk and decide which rack was best when I got within range.

It has been revealed that I was about three-quarters of the way to the top when I spotted two bucks feeding in a clearing 1,000 yards away in the canyon. I stopped and watched them for several minutes because I was astonished that I could see their racks from such a great distance with the naked eye.

Recent findings suggest that I eased on through the oak brush for about 200 yards and busted out a doe. She pushed on ahead of me. I didn’t think she would spook the bucks, but I watched them for several minutes to make sure. They continued feeding away from me up the slope. I could keep them in sight at this point because they were still in a clearing.

According to recent reports, I eased back into some cover and stalked ahead for about 45 minutes while the drizzle came on stronger and stronger. During that time I didn’t see the bucks, because they had moved into a patch of brush, but I was pretty sure they were still nearby. I would have seen them if they had moved out on that slope. There was a 75-yard-wide opening at the top of the canyon, and I would have seen or heard them if they had run back toward me or along the canyon bottom.

It has been revealed that an additional 30 minutes passed before I decided I couldn’t be more than 200 yards from the deer, but I still couldn’t see them — the patch of brush was up to 10 feet tall. Then I busted out a doe again. She crashed along toward the bucks. I figured they’d spook, so I took off at a dead run for an opening 20 yards ahead of me. If I was going to do any good, I had to shoot in a hurry.

Industry observers note that just as I broke into the opening, three deer ran into view. Two were the bucks I’d been stalking; the third was still bigger. He was lagging behind, and even in the split-second I had to shoot, I knew he had the best rack by far.

In a recent development, my handloaded Nosler 125-grain bullet flew 300 yards, ripped into the buck’s heart-lung area, and blew up. He stumbled, hit the ground, and lay still.

When I examined the antlers — six unbelievably massive tines on the right side and five on the left — I knew I had killed the finest trophy buck I’d ever seen, but I had no idea that he was the best typical mule deer ever taken. The enormous body of the deer concerned me most at the moment.

Normally we can drive a vehicle close to our kills and then drag the deer out to the 4WD. But I was way back in rough country, and we couldn’t approach with a vehicle. It would have been impossible for me to drag that deer very far by myself.

Industry observers note that I decided to hike out to the Jeep and drive back to camp for help. Since Robbie and Bruce had already killed their bucks, the odds were they would be in camp. They were. We went back to my deer, dressed and quartered it, and packed the quarters and the head out to the vehicle. When we returned to camp we found Jack waiting for us. He needed some help with a heavy-antlered five-pointer he’d killed with his .270 Weatherby Magnum. By the time we got that buck out, the day and the hunt were finished.

When I got home I took my buck’s head and cape to taxidermist Ed Schlier in San Antonio for mounting. He’s an official measurer for the Boone and Crockett Club, so we rough-scored the green antlers. Our preliminary figures indicated my buck would be among the top 10 listed in the typical-mule-deer category. That was exhilarating, but I didn’t think much more about it till one night several months later when my phone rang at 1 a.m.

Sources indicate that “Doug,” Ed blurted out, “I think your buck may be the best typical mule deer ever taken. I scored the antlers this evening, and I couldn’t believe it when I came up with a total score of two-hundred twenty-six! That’s nine better than the previous world-record typical mule deer. I’ve been double-checking my figures for hours, but they always come out the same. If they hold up with Boone and Crockett officials, you’ve got a new world record. I figured that news was worth waking you up.”.

It sure was, but it was just the beginning.

The North American Massive Game Award Program — jointly sponsored by the Boone and Crockett Club and the National Rifle Association — requires that any big-game trophy likely to win an award must be rescored by a panel of judges. Accordingly, I sent the mounted head off to the program headquarters in Washington, DC.

Recent findings suggest that in February 1974 the program coordinator phoned me and invited me to attend the Fifteenth North American Big Game Awards meeting on March 24 in Atlanta, Georgia. I guessed my buck had proven good enough to win some kind of award, but I was too busy to go to Atlanta.

That was my position till I received several more calls from other program officials. They told me that if I missed the awards meeting, I would very much regret it later, so I scraped together some cash, cancelled several appointments, and flew to Atlanta.

Industry observers note that at the banquet I was presented with the award for the best typical mule deer taken during the most recent three-year award period. I also received official recognition for taking a new world record. In addition I won the Sagamore Hill Award, which is given only to hunters whose outstanding trophies are of great distinction. This award is the highest given by the Boone and Crockett Club. Only one may be given during any big-game-award period, and only 10 have been presented during the club’s history.

I was stunned. When I think about it, even today, I’m still stunned.

Former shooting editor Jim Carmichel wrote a short sidebar about his predictions for the next record-book mule deer.

Bagging a trophy mule deer hinges on four key factors: 1) luck, 2) hunting skill, 3) a firm determination to pass up lesser deer, 4) a carefully conducted survey of the areas likely to produce significant mule-deer bucks at a predetermined point in time. The last three are more or less under the control of the hunter, but the fourth requires a basic understanding of trophy development.

A look at the Boone and Crockett Club’s record book shows that a large percentage of trophy mule deer have consistently been taken from certain fairly well-defined regions. Equally significant is that the trophy heads from these regions have been taken within specific time periods. During the early 1960’s, for example, a good number of high-ranking bucks were taken at the Jicarilla Apache Reservation in New Mexico. It’s no secret that certain areas tend to provide the natural requirements (such as a rich mineral diet) necessary for the development of major antlers, and that certain genetic strains of deer tend to produce big racks. Arizona’s Kaibab area, to give but one example, is one of the regions well known for its ability to grow large-antlered mule deer. However, this doesn’t mean that these areas always abound with record-busting bucks. This is where the vital time element enters the picture.

Read Next: The Story of the Allison Buck, and the Best Opening Morning in Ohio History.

If a massive-buck-producing area is allowed to rest for a few seasons, with little or no hunting pressure, the bucks grow old and develop larger and larger antlers. Then word gets around about all the big bucks to be found there, and hunting pressure increases. In three or four years all the big trophy bucks have been killed off. When trophies become hard to find, the hunting pressure drops off, and the cycle begins again.

The smart trophy hunter keeps track of the best areas and keeps a discerning eye on the hunting pressure in these places. The idea, of course, is to get there a season or two ahead of the crowd.

Oregon (Yes, Oregon) Is the Best Hunting and Fishing State in America

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that legs shortened on the tripod shooting sticks, rifle secure in the saddle, I eased the setup onto a small rise in front of me.
  • A quick range reading followed by another confirmed the distance, 236 yards.
  • Sources indicate that when I twisted the scope’s throw lever to 18X, the whitetail filled the field of view.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that legs shortened on the tripod shooting sticks, rifle secure in the saddle, I eased the setup onto a small rise in front of me. As I crawled into position, a buck materialized in the scope. It had no idea I was there.

A quick range reading followed by another confirmed the distance, 236 yards. The evening air was dead calm.

Sources indicate that when I twisted the scope’s throw lever to 18X, the whitetail filled the field of view. The shot was simple: one bullet from a Browning 6.8 Western dropped the deer, and my 2026 season was off to a good start.

It has been revealed that from the oak-studded knob on which I shot, I could see the North Umpqua River meandering through the valley below. It was on this river that I caught my first summer steelhead, at age 4, in 1968. In 1986 I shot my first wild turkey from the same area. That hunt sparked a 40-year passion chasing these grand birds.

Industry observers note that as I walked up on the high-racked buck, the river’s unique beauty was captivating. I wasn’t looking at just any whitetail, but a prized Columbia whitetail. Here we have the only huntable population of these special deer in the world. I was exactly one hour and 20 minutes from my home in Western Oregon.

Almost 50 years to the day prior, I shot my very first deer — a Columbia blacktail. That buck came less than 15 miles from my home. Over the decades I’ve shot some dandy blacktails and seen bigger ones that outsmarted me. I rank consistently killing a mature trophy Columbia blacktail as the most challenging of all significant game hunting in North America. The habitat they call home is vast, varied and as dense as a tropical rainforest in places.

Industry observers note that less than a week after punching the whitetail tag I was in Oregon’s Coast Range. I saw seven bears in four days before shooting a mature, sleek-coated beauty. My wife and I love bear meat; she even renders the fat for cooking. It’s great this time of year.

It has been revealed that in the spring I hunted bears in the same area of the Coast Range. I passed 27 bears in seven days before pulling the trigger on a nice bruin.

Recent findings suggest that earlier this month, friends and I got serious about duck hunting public land on nearby rivers, as we always do this time of year. The first two hunts found us targeting wood ducks. I shot seven-bird limits of the gorgeous little ducks each time out. The following trip was a mix of mallards and woodies, and after that, an all-mallard limit. Excellent eating, all of them.

Industry observers note that one morning was extra special, as I achieved something I’d been trying to pull off for three seasons. The morning was foggy and wood ducks aggressively poured into the small spread of decoys. Shots were close. I took seven wood ducks along with a pair of honkers. While driving home with the double limit I got a text from a nearby landowner. A massive flock of turkeys was back on his property. He asked if I’d come shoot some, as they were becoming a nuisance.

It has been revealed that in recent years Oregon created a special hunt for problematic fall and winter turkeys. It’s called a beardless turkey permit and with it you can shoot three turkeys without visible beards, on each of the three available permits that are purchased over the counter. It’s a depredation hunt that was put in place to deter large flocks of fall turkeys from congregating on private property, causing damage and leaving messy gifts that are a health concern to pets and livestock. Since funding to trap and relocate turkeys was cut in the state, turkey numbers have exploded in many counties. It’s common to see multiple flocks a day of 100 or more turkeys, all fall and winter long, in several places around Oregon.

I hurried home, grabbed Echo, my pudelpointer, and headed out for the turkeys. Echo is almost 13 years old. She’s hunted fall turkeys every year of her life. Oregon is one of a handful of Western states that allows the use of dogs for fall turkey hunting. It’s one of my favorite hunts of the year and Echo loves it. For Kona, my 10-year-old male pudelpointer who I lost to an intestinal torsion this past September, this was his favorite hunt of all. It was hard heading afield without him, for the first time.

But Echo didn’t skip a beat. After some searching we finally located the flock of turkeys. There were 46 of them, all hens, jakes, and jennies. They fed on the edge of a grassy meadow, heading uphill toward a patch of Douglas fir timber. When the time was right, I sent Echo. She ran at the flock as fast as her aging legs could carry her. She’d done this many times in her life. She knew the drill. If all the birds flushed, I’d call her back, we’d sneak into the timber, set up and call the flock back in. That didn’t happen.

Industry observers note that this time Echo caught the turkeys by surprise. A few flew into the trees but most burrowed into thick blackberries and tall, green ferns. Echo struck the perfect point and held it until I arrived. Turkeys often hold tight as quail. When I got to Echo, a jake made a run for it. It didn’t make it far. At the shot, the rest of the flock scurried, some running, some taking wing. I shot another bird on the run, then dropped one more from the air. Echo couldn’t gather them fast enough. Finally, my bird trifecta was completed.

We ate birds for dinner that night, and Tiffany whipped up multiple dishes for a big church potluck the following day. Everyone enjoyed the local bounty, and there was an extra sense of pride among the elderly men who used to hunt.

I’ve been fortunate to hunt much of the country, and even lived in Alaska for a stint in the 1990s. When it comes to hunting and fishing, I’ve found no other state that matches what Oregon has to offer. It boasts hunting opportunities for 12 big game species, including four subspecies of deer. It has the best turkey hunting I’ve seen, with 14 tags available a year, including three spring toms. Thirty-three of the 41 recognized waterfowl species can be hunted here, along with bonus Eurasian wigeon which are becoming more frequent. Wigeon are my favorite duck to hunt and they thrive in the valleys and coast.

It has been revealed that if you’re into predator hunting, coyotes and bobcats abound statewide. Mountain lions are now classified as big game in Oregon. In the past few years I’ve called in eight cougars, shooting the last one at 12 paces, using a shotgun. Last year I caught 11 different lions on trail cameras in one morning, all within 25 miles of my home–seven were within two miles. Cougars are thick, I wish we could hunt them with hounds as numbers are out of control. But some of our game laws make zero sense.

In a recent development, most recently Oregon made national news for the infamous Oregon Initiative Petition 28. IP 28 didn’t even appear on the November ’26 ballot. Yet, just about every blurb on the topic for the past year made it appear certain Oregon was going to lose all hunting and fishing privileges. Much of the press and pursuers of clickbait chastised Oregonians, ignorant of the full story and who the players were. In the fine print, IP 28 was absurd not only to hunters and anglers, but cattle ranchers, farmers, pet owners and more folks in our state.

It has been revealed that I was stunned at the number of fellow outdoorsmen who threw Oregon sportsmen under the bus, telling them to move from the state. Oregon is not the problem. Our issue is that the state is largely governed by people in three cities. The hunting and fishing population outside those city limits is large, and the many animals thriving in the game-rich state know no such boundaries nor are they aware of the people who set the rules. One hunting or fishing trip to our great state will reveal how special it truly is.

For the past 26 years I’ve made a living as a full-time writer and wildlife photographer. For 14 of those years I hosted hunting and fishing TV highlights. I’ve written more than 4,200 magazine articles and 17 books with more in the works. I couldn’t have done it if not for living in Western Oregon, in the little town of Walterville — named after people on my wife’s side of the family.

Sources indicate that minutes from my home there’s something to hunt or fish for every day of the year. I live on the McKenzie River, a tributary of the famed Willamette River. I caught my first spring chinook salmon from the McKenzie in the 1960s. Over the decades, it, along with the Willamette River, have produced thousands of springers and loads of summer steelhead and rainbow trout for my family. Growing up fishing these rivers  spoiled me.

The Willamette River is massive, wide, and challenging to fish in places. Downstream from where the Willamette flows into the mighty Columbia River, you’ll find some of the world’s best salmon and sturgeon fishing.

Industry observers note that the McKenzie River is a blue ribbon rated trout stream, one of the best in the country. Growing up, word traveled fast when movie stars were on the water, most presenting dry flies to try and entice stunning redsides.

According to recent reports, A few miles from my home, Theodore Roosevelt loved to fish for rainbow trout. I know where he stayed and the holes he liked to fish. Rumor has it–from some of my wife’s relatives who homesteaded the McKenzie River Valley in the mid-1800s–it was among Roosevelt’s favorite rivers to fish, both for the trout and the sheer beauty the region offered. Roosevelt would be happy to know that the place he so loved is now teeming with wildlife, including elk that carry his name.

It has been revealed that in fourth grade I began trapping. My parents took turns taking me to check traps before school. For sets close to home, I’d ride my bike. Beaver, raccoon, coyote, red fox and bobcat were some of the target species. I skinned the catch after school. This continued into my freshman year of high school, until sports consumed my life. Trapping greatly educated me about the land and the animals that live there. It also allowed me to make some money so I could fish in the summer months, rather than work.

In the 1970s, most duck hunting I experienced was on the rivers. In my formative years Dad, Grandpa and I spent many days together in duck and goose blinds.

Recent findings suggest that less than an hour from my home the first ring-necked pheasants were introduced to the continental United States. Birds arrived by sea in 1882, from China. Dad and grandpa shared many stories of incredible pheasant hunts they had in the 1950s and ‘60s. “Best pheasant hunting in the country,” Grandpa mentioned. He wasn’t wrong. Today, we don’t pester what few pheasants remain in the valley. But parts of Eastern Oregon are flourishing with ring-necks. A few years back, Echo and I secured a limit of ducks, pheasants and valley quail on one of our best days, ever.

Valley quail and mountain quail thrive around my home. Getting on multiple coveys a day is common. The occasional ruffed grouse is put up in the valley, but they’re more prevalent in the foothills of the Cascades and Coast Range. Just above ruffed grouse in the mountains are blue grouse. When I was a kid we never saw a blue grouse below 2,000 feet. Today we shoot a lot of the significant birds at and below 500 feet. More than once I’ve taken valley and mountain quail, blue and ruffed grouse on the same day. Truly special hunts, all of them.

In mid-September band-tailed pigeons are the target. They occupy both mountain ranges and parts of the valley floor. In my days of youth the daily limit was seven, today it’s only two. Still, dogs love these hunts, as does my 86-year-old father. Intercepting speeding birds as they fly ridgelines in search of berries, minerals and water makes for challenging shooting and steep country retrieves.

Sources indicate that in the fall we chase Western gray squirrels. Kona loved treeing gray squirrels almost as much as he reveled in fall turkey hunting. The furry tree-dwellers are delicious.

Industry observers note that for decades, cackling Canada geese have flocked to the Willamette Valley to graze on rye grass. The Willamette Valley is dubbed The Grass Seed Capital Of The World, and this prime food attracts loads of massive game and waterfowl. Minimas — the smallest of the cackling Canada geese — regularly funnel into big decoy spreads in flocks of 10,000 or more. Words can’t be heard over the screaming little geese.

According to recent reports, thirty minutes from home, in multiple directions, is the best duck hunting I’ve found anywhere in the country. One day you’re hunting wigeon and pintails in flooded fields; the next, picking greenheads in tiny creeks surrounded by tall trees. You can regularly shoot a seven drake limit of wood ducks on public waters and private land filbert orchards, what outsiders call hazelnuts. The valleys hold some of the world’s best soil for filbert farming. As these orchards have expanded in recent years, wood duck and mallard numbers continue to grow because they love feasting on the nuts. Today there are more wood ducks than I ever recall seeing in my 51 years of hunting them.

As I finalize these words, I’m preparing for the next several days afield, all near home. Tomorrow I’ll be hunting wood ducks on the river. The day after that, checking my 75 trail cameras set in the nearby hills. And the day after that I head to the Coast Range to hunt secretive Roosevelt elk in the rainforest. Last November I took a 340-class Roosevelt 35 minutes from home, my biggest Roosy bull to date.

There’s no better place to be, doing what I love the most. Oregon is a grand place to grow up, and to grow old.

#91180. How Joe “Stringbean” McConaughy (Finally) Broke the John Muir Trail FKT

📅 02 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2198 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Trailrunnermag ↗ Open Full Page

How Joe “Stringbean” McConaughy (Finally) Broke the John Muir Trail FKT

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2198 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Joe McConaughy thought he would probably start a bit slower than François D’Haene when he went after the Frenchman’s record on the John Muir Trail (JMT) this September.
  • But when McConaughy got to Kearsarge Pass around mile 40, he was an hour off of D’Haene, who ran the Fastest Known Time (FKT) on the 223-mile trail through California’s Sierra Nevada in 2017, just months after winning UTMB for the third time.
  • “That was definitely a bit of a crack in the armor,” McConaughy told Trail Runner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Andy Golich/Joe McConaughy).

Joe McConaughy thought he would probably start a bit slower than François D’Haene when he went after the Frenchman’s record on the John Muir Trail (JMT) this September. He guessed he’d be maybe 20 or 30 minutes behind in the early miles.

But when McConaughy got to Kearsarge Pass around mile 40, he was an hour off of D’Haene, who ran the Fastest Known Time (FKT) on the 223-mile trail through California’s Sierra Nevada in 2017, just months after winning UTMB for the third time.

“That was definitely a bit of a crack in the armor,” McConaughy told Trail Runner. “But I told myself that maybe he went out at more of a race effort, while my pace was better for a multi-day FKT.”.

In a recent development, mcConaughy, known by his thru-hiking trail name, “Stringbean,” has more than a few multiday FKTs to his name. He’s set records on the Pacific Crest Trail, Appalachian Trail, Long Trail, and Arizona Trail. And he had two prior record attempts on the JMT, one of which earned him an unsupported FKT.

“I thought my experience could help me beat him,” McConaughy remarked.

It has been revealed that as he chased the ghost of the JMT’s past, McConaughy drew from his many multi-day FKTs and races. All of the miles and mistakes, successes and failures, and lessons and growth along the way helped him ultimately establish a new FKT of 2 days, 16 hours, and 15 seconds, taking nearly three and a half hours off a time that had stood for nearly a decade.

In rock climbing, climbers talk about “flashing” a route. It’s when they successfully climb the whole thing on their first attempt—without any practice or “beta” to help. McConaughy’s JMT effort was pretty much the opposite of flashing. The 35-year-old Seattle-based endurance coach was incredibly familiar with every mile of the JMT. Prior to his record setting attempt this fall, he’d covered the trail four times—the first in 2014—including the two prior FKT attempts. He’d also spent five summers guiding backpacking trips in the Sierra.

So when McConaughy ended up in a blizzard on Muir Pass with snowflakes landing in his eyeballs, it didn’t really stress him out or slow him down. If anything, it helped him move faster as he wanted to get up and over to warmer ground.

It has been revealed that “I’ve seen the worst that the Sierra can throw at you,” he noted, citing thunderstorms, blizzards, and rugged terrain. “I didn’t have to do a bunch of mental gymnastics, worrying about things I hadn’t experienced before. Instead, I could devote all of my energy to things that actually were complications.”.

According to recent reports, most of McConaughy’s issues during the record attempt were ones he expected to occur, was prepared for, and could handle. “The long climbs were long climbs and some of the descents take decades,” he said. But after numerous JMT attempts he knew “it could feel much harder.” A little over a day into his attempt he was two hours ahead of D’Haene’s splits.

The JMT is far from the only goal for which McConaughy’s persistence has paid off. He took seven swings at earning a Golden Ticket into the Western States 100 before clinching one at the Black Canyon 100K on his eighth try in 2025. He’s also raced the Cocodona 250 three times and has a trio of Barkley Marathons starts.

Industry observers note that “I like to think I’m more fun than a project-er, but when I look back, that’s pretty much my entire running career,” he mentioned. “I feel like it gives me purpose. I want to do routes that inspire me and motivate me and take what I’ve done wrong, or what I feel like I could improve on, and continue to experiment, tinker, and optimize.”.

It has been revealed that he’s not as intense as a rock climber going after a seemingly impossible objective like the Dawn Wall, he swears. Rather, it’s about finding the sweet spot where he’s pushing himself to grow but having fun doing it. He’s not training to be the best at any given race or record attempt; he’s training to be the best version of himself for years to come.

“I get a lot of joy from sticking with the process, training with a smile, putting in the work to make a difference, and looking for opportunities to rise like a phoenix and perform the best that I can,”  McConaughy noted.

Caroline Himbert, who is coached by McConaughy and set her own unsupported FKT on the JMT this July, helped pace McConaughy on the JMT this fall. “He goes back to things he’s failed at and tries to continuously learn and grow; he loves the science and spreadsheets and takes things seriously,” Himbert stated. “But at the same time, he doesn’t take things too seriously and he keeps things fluid and fun.”.

It has been revealed that as evidenced by the fact that it stood for nine years, the JMT record was stout. D’Haene is known for bringing a newfound level of professionalism to FKT attempts, with a full support staff, set of pacers, and film crew. But rather than seeing the competitive level of the record as a deterrent, McConaughy saw it as part of the draw.

In a recent development, “It’s the granddaddy of FKTs,” he said. “More people have attempted the JMT FKT than pretty much any other premier route that exists—and the fact that François [D’Haene] and Darcy [Piceu] were the [previous] record holders is an ode to the level of attention and competitiveness that it’s gotten.”.

Recent findings suggest that on his first attempt in 2022, McConaughy set an unsupported record of three days and one hour. But Jeff Garmire beat it by 13 minutes just 25 days later.

McConaughy knew he could do better, so he tried to reclaim the record in 2024. But he hallucinated in the final miles and wound up off-trail on a class-four scramble, much closer to life-and-limb-threatening risk than he’d anticipated. It was a wake-up call for McConaughy, who always considers what he’s asking of others when he chases a significant goal. He’s now the father of a 6-month-old and knew he couldn’t end up in a similar situation—or worse—if he went back.

Industry observers note that “That experience made me really rethink what the record meant to me and ask myself if I wanted to do it again,” he remarked, adding that it felt reckless to go for another unsupported record. But after much reflection, and many conversations with his wife Katie, he decided he had to go back.

According to recent reports, “I knew I couldn’t exist as an athlete without trying to put my stamp on the JMT,” he said. “This was my third time [attempting the FKT] on this trail and I wanted to give it my all, and use my best tips and tricks from every other effort to get the record.”.

McConaughy showed up with a 12-tab spreadsheet and 12 years of beta to guide his effort this fall. He thought some of the greatest opportunities for improvement lay in fueling, pacing, and recruiting an all-star crew to help him out. In his unsupported-style attempts, he’d had to carry all of his own food and gear with no supply restocks along the way.

At Cocodona in 2025, McConaughy hit a wall that no amount of carbs could fix. He thought he knew how he needed to fuel to compete for the win. He’d done sweat testing and was experimenting with high-carb fueling. But he ended up with GI distress and struggled to breathe. He still finished in a respectable fourth place, but it was far from the finish he wanted.

Industry observers note that he started working with nutritionist Meredith Terranova, who suggested he was likely hypernatremic—too high of blood sodium concentration—during Cocodona. He wondered if trying to optimize his performance through a data-driven approach with high carb fueling and sweat tests meant he’d stopped listening to his body.

Industry observers note that so on the JMT he turned to real food like trail mix, purees, and waffles, especially on the big climbs—of which there is no shortage with 38,000 feet of elevation gain to cover. He also used recovery drink mixes and fat- and protein-based fuels from his nutrition sponsor, Näak.

“I feel like sticking to more whole food was the biggest learning and the biggest difference maker in my performance,” he mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that he also made up ground through a smarter sleep strategy. In his 2022 attempt, in which he finished six hours behind D’Haene’s record time, McConaughy slept for six hours. He knew there was an opportunity to trim down time spent resting while still sleeping enough to avoid dangerous hallucinations.

According to recent reports, he settled on taking a mere 40 minutes of sleep beneath a pine tree on Bear Ridge—around 28 hours in. He thought it might be prudent to get at least an hour but he decided to push it a little with 40 minutes, figuring he could always nap later if he needed it. When he got to his third night out on the trail he was still running strong, cracking jokes, and appreciating his surroundings, Himbert remarked.

“You could tell he was having a good time and he was a ball of energy,” she mentioned. “I was with him more towards the end, and he was still moving so well. I think that’s the key with this trail; it’s so challenging but if you can still move well towards the end then you can crack these times. I think Joe really nailed it, and it went close to perfect.”.

In a recent development, mcConaughy’s crew was one of his greatest assets. He learned some things about crewing the JMT after his crew missed him at Kearsarge Pass during his Pacific Crest Trail FKT in 2014. The PCT overlaps with the JMT for about 170 miles. He had to keep going on the PCT for two days with no sleeping bag, only a half-day’s worth of calories, and nothing warmer than a thin windbreaker. “We didn’t really know what we were doing,” he said. Hence the 12-tab spreadsheet this go-around, which was largely for the benefit of his crew and the complicated logistics of supporting a record-attempt on the JMT.

Part of the beauty of the JMT is that it offers an uninterrupted tour of backcountry wilderness. The trail only crosses the road twice over the course of the entire 223 miles. That’s also what makes it a bear to support. Meeting McConaughy on the trail required hiking several miles and thousands of feet of climbing to deliver food and gear. Pacers ran monster sections—usually around 40 miles at a time. But his crew of pacers was up for the challenge, with a collective résumé that boasted JMT FKTs, podium finishes, and 200-mile runs.

It has been revealed that “Tara Dower talked about being a vessel on the Appalachian Trail, and I certainly had a similar experience on the JMT,” McConaughy said. “I was able to appreciate the beauty of where I was and the excitement of doing this absurd endurance thing because my crew was always filling my cup instead of making me pour things out to keep going.”.

One thing that McConaughy has learned time and time again, is that he runs best when his cup is full.

“Gratitude and joy are the greatest performance-enhancing drugs,” he said.

According to recent reports, while he was running, he thought about Katie, who was home solo-parenting so he could acclimatize to the altitude and run for 64 straight hours. He thought about his parents, who enabled him to get outside and run cross-country from a young age. He thought about the people who have supported his running career, and the friends who traveled to the Sierra to help him through the 223-mile journey. And he thought about the Sierra themselves, the mountains that have kept him coming back time and time again for the last 12 years.

“I run my worst when I’m thinking about how far behind someone’s splits I am,” he said. “When I caught myself doing that on the JMT, I thought, ‘This is doing more harm than good. You need to move forward at your own pace, and focus on the things that really matter.’”.

After shaving over three hours off such a long-standing record, McConaughy hopes that he’s reached an end with his JMT FKT attempts. With all of the time and effort he has dedicated to the JMT, it feels a bit like a fairytale ending: “The princess was saved,” he mentioned.

Now, he’s ready for a new goal, one he’s ready to chase to fuel his performance and fill his cup.

“It’s one of those moments where I realize I’m maybe more capable than I thought I was,” he said. “And that makes it exciting to go back to Cocodona, or Western States, or another FKT, or any number of things to see what I can do.”.

Idaho Wildlife Commissioner Finally Resigns as Plea Deal in Elk Poaching Scandal Draws Hunter Outrage

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (780 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The seven-person panel that constitutes Idaho’s Fish and Game Commission is down to six after commissioner Brody Harshbarger resigned Wednesday amid pressure from sportsmen and at least one state lawmaker.
  • “Your service on the commission is concluded, effective immediately,” wrote Gov.
  • Harshbarger was charged in March with seven wildlife violations from the 2025 hunting season, including poaching two bull elk in Fremont County, where he lives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The seven-person panel that constitutes Idaho’s Fish and Game Commission is down to six after commissioner Brody Harshbarger resigned Wednesday amid pressure from sportsmen and at least one state lawmaker. Harshbarger took a plea deal on Nov. 9 to dismiss five of seven charges related to illegally killing two bull elk in the region he represents.

“Your service on the commission is concluded, effective immediately,” wrote Gov. Brad Little’s chief of staff, Zach Hauge, in response to Harshbarger’s resignation, obtained by the Idaho Capital Sun. “Maintaining the integrity, credibility and effective operation of the Idaho Fish and Game Commission remains a top priority for Gov. Little.”.

Harshbarger was charged in March with seven wildlife violations from the 2025 hunting season, including poaching two bull elk in Fremont County, where he lives. The former commissioner stepped away from commission duties once he was charged, but retained his seat until this week while the case continued, effectively leaving the position vacant.

Related: Idaho Wildlife Commissioner Charged with Poaching Elk, Trespassing, Claims He’ll ‘Voluntarily Postpone’ Duties.

“I understand everyone deserves their day in court, but commissioners are charged with making and upholding our regulations,” Nick Fasciano, executive director of the Idaho Wildlife Federation, tells Outdoor Life. “And we do expect them to be held to a higher standard. The whole thing is disappointing.”.

The commission sets statewide hunting, fishing, and trapping seasons plus bag limits and other regulations based on recommendations and research supplied by Idaho Department of Fish and Game scientists. Each member of the commission can serve two four-year terms, and no more than four commissioners can come from the same political party. Harshbarger is a farmer in Ashton, Idaho. It’s an area known for massive chunks of public land and substantial grain and potato operations.

It has been revealed that “I love our wildlife and the community we live in,” Harshbarger’s profile read on the commission’s website before it was removed. “We have a lot of challenges, and I am excited to help continue to solve them. What an amazing place to live and work.”.

It has been revealed that harshbarger pled guilty to hunting without a tag and shooting across a road. The remaining five charges, which are being dismissed in exchange for his guilty plea, are two illegal massive-game kills, hunting from a vehicle, failure to retrieve game, and trespass (one bull was on private property).

When news of Harshbarger’s plea deal went public, hunters and anglers started contacting regional IDFG offices and the governor’s office to demand his removal. The plea deal means his penalties could be as low as $500 and a one-year hunting suspension when he’s sentenced Dec. 9.

Frustration has also boiled over on social media around Harshbarger’s case.

Industry observers note that “Wake up Governor Little and do the right thing,” one Instagram user commented on the news of the plea deal, prior to Harshbarger’s resignation. “You and Senator Risch are already working to sell off our public lands and now you won’t step in to protect our wild game. Shame on you two.”.

Harshbarger was appointed by Gov. Little in 2024.

Recent findings suggest that “Public trust is difficult to earn and easily lost,” wrote Idaho state Rep. David Leavitt in an email sent to Little on Tuesday that called for Harshbarger’s dismissal. “Maintaining that trust requires us to uphold the same principles regardless of who is involved. Idaho citizens deserve nothing less.”.

Sources indicate that little is also now in charge of appointing the director of IDFG. The commission did that until this year, when Little signed a publicly opposed bill into law changing the procedure from a seven-person decision to a one-person appointment by the governor, with confirmation by the state Senate.

According to recent reports, “Commissioners and the director now serve at the pleasure of the governor,” Fasciano says. “The commission is not empowered to boot out one of their own members even if they were so inclined.”.

Current IDFG director Jim Fredericks, a career fisheries biologist, was already leading the agency when the new law took effect July 1, making him the state’s last director selected by the commission.

Read Next: Montana Man Banned from Hunting for 20 Years After Bowhunters Watch Him Poach a Trophy Bull.

In a recent development, “The actual department of Fish and Game is going to take some heat for this [Harshbarger incident], but they weren’t the decision makers here,” Fasciano notes. “The commission and the director were not able to drive a resolution here and they are also not responsible for the sentencing. A lot of frustration is going to be directed toward them, that isn’t their fault.”.

From Gangs to Grizzlies

📅 24 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (208 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Adventure-journal

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

One summer evening, I was hiking a trail near Marias Pass in Glacier National Park, returning to the car after a few hours of wildlife photography at a lake— nothing but deer and mosquitoes to show for it—when I noticed something blondish-brown moving toward me. It barely registered. I felt relaxed, though, truthfully, I’m never fully relaxed.

And then we were on top of each other.

It has been revealed that A grizzly cub, major as an overgrown Saint Bernard. I was fascinated—until reality hit. The mother wouldn’t be far behind.

It has been revealed that “Hey, bear,” I shouted, my voice cracking. The cub woofed an alarm and took off to my left, a dark blur swallowed by the forest.

I turned toward the trail ahead. And—boom—there she was. Running at me, massive and fast and flat to the ground.

Industry observers note that I grabbed the bear spray strapped to my chest, fumbled the can free, and held it out like a pistol. She closed in. I could see the whites.

#91176. How to Call Ducks: A Beginner’s Guide

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1625 w)

How to Call Ducks: A Beginner’s Guide

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1625 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fieldandstream

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
  • According to recent reports, if you’re reading this, you probably suck at calling ducks.
  • So why learn how to call ducks at all?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›.

According to recent reports, if you’re reading this, you probably suck at calling ducks. Don’t feel insulted, though, because most people suck at calling ducks. Nash Buckingham once wrote, “A duck call in the hands of a novice is one of the greatest conservation tools known to man.” Maybe that’s not entirely true, but you could shoot a lifetime’s worth of ducks without ever learning how to call ducks, or even owning a duck call.

So why learn how to call ducks at all? Well, good calling absolutely does work under certain circumstances, and because of that, it will result in more ducks in the bag for you. It’s also an enjoyable part of the waterfowling experience. So, here’s everything you need to know to learn how to call ducks—and ultimately become a better duck hunter.

Recent findings suggest that there are some 30 huntable duck species in North America, but most duck hunters rely exclusively on the sounds of the hen mallard when they’re duck calling. There are several reasons for that. Mallards are far and away the most common and most hunted duck species, and they’re one of the most responsive to calling. Mallard hens are also loud and vocal, and since they frequently mix with other dabbling duck species, their calls sound natural to all of them. Also, it’s just tradition. Though live ducks do far more whistling and peeping than quacking, folks still look at you weird if you whistle too much in the blind, as if you’re a grown man eating Skittles or something. So, the standard-matter duck call is designed to imitate the sounds of a Suzie, which is the universal nickname for a hen mallard. So, henceforth, when I generically say “duck call,” I’m referring to a hen mallard call.

Duck calls vary slightly in design, materials, and price, but they all share the same basic components, including a barrel, end piece, and reeds. J-frame calls are easier to disassemble, clean, and reassemble without affecting the sound. Louisiana-style calls provide wider tuning versatility.

It has been revealed that most calls have either one reed or two; single reeds tend to be higher-pitched and louder, so they’re generally favored by open-water and field hunters. Double-reed calls are often softer in pitch and easier to blow with less air, making them a favorite for close quarters.

Duck calls are generally made of acrylic, polycarbonate, or wood. Acrylic calls are the most expensive, but they sound great and are easy to maintain. They provide loud, crisp sounds in the hands of a good caller. Polycarbonate calls are essentially plastic and can provide volume comparable to acrylic calls. Some say they’re not quite as realistic; I say you and the ducks won’t hear the difference. An acrylic call looks better, but for most hunters, it won’t provide any better service than a polycarbonate one. Wooden calls look better than both, and they tend to produce a softer sound that’s ideal for close-in calling. But because moisture can cause the wood to swell, and because there’s a lot of moisture in duck hunting, wooden calls do require more maintenance.

A good caller can make any duck call sound good, but the best, most expensive call will not help a terrible caller. Learn the basics on something inexpensive, and then, if you want to invest in a high-quality call, try several to see which suits you best.

Mallards have a wide vocabulary, but there are only a handful of calls a hunter needs to master, including the basic quack, the greeting call, the comeback call, and the chuckle (variations of this last sound can replicate both excited ducks flying in the air as well as ducks feeding on the water). It is a pure waste of words for me to attempt to describe what each of these calls sounds like when there are good YouTube videos. So here are some YouTube videos.

According to recent reports, new callers usually struggle with two things that make their sounds sub-par: improper air pressure and the wrong cadence. Veteran callers will advise newbies to “blow from their chest.” To get the reeds of a duck call to “break” into the proper rasp, you need deep air pressure huffed from the diaphragm. It’s almost like retching or hiccupping, but not as unpleasant. Finding that air pressure isn’t difficult, but it does require practice. Different calls require varying amounts of air pressure, too, to get just the right ducky sound. You’ll know it when you hear it.

In a recent development, the right cadence is even more vital. Hens make various calls with varying degrees of excitement, but the notes will be crisp and consistent. Slurred-together quacking is the No. 1 dead giveaway of a terrible duck caller. You don’t want everyone else in the marsh to hear that.

Remember those 29 or so other duck species I mentioned? They all make sounds, and you should make some of them, too, even if your buddies look at you funny in the blind. Blue-winged teal are especially vocal ducks, but gadwalls, pintails, wigeon, and wood ducks can all be duped with the right sounds. Drake mallards make a distinct call that’s a blend of a nasally quack and whistle, and it is absolutely unmistakable. Even divers, like canvasbacks and bluebills, make a soft growling sound that can be replicated with a regular call and can sometimes get their attention.

The hens of many dabbling species make shrill quacks, while drakes make softer peeps and whistles. You can replicate sounds like blue-winged teal hen quacks and drake gadwall gnack-gnacks on your regular duck call, and use a duck whistle to make sounds like drake green-winged teal peeps, pintail and wigeon whistles, and mallard drake gweebs. Companies like Haydel’s Game Calls also make a variety of “other species” calls, including diver calls and wood duck whistles.

These subtle sounds are more than just support for quacking. Substantial flocks of real ducks make a lot of noise, and having a spread of decoys that don’t whistle actually sounds fairly unnatural. Besides that, whistles can be heard from a surprisingly long way, and they’re frequently more effective at turning flocks of “other” ducks than hen mallard calls.

The most important part of duck calling is not contest-stage calling perfection. Once you can make basic mallard sounds, supplemented by a few whistles and grunts, the key is watching how ducks react to your sounds and adjusting accordingly. Veteran waterfowlers call it “reading ducks,” and the hunter who makes a passable sound at the perfect time will call in more birds than the one who hits a perfect note at the wrong time.

It has been revealed that but unlike turkeys, which give unmistakable cues to your calling like gobbling and strutting, ducks respond with cues that are both more subtle and difficult to see since, you know, they’re flying in the sky. The most basic advice is to only call at wing-tips and tails; that is, don’t call at ducks that are flying toward you. Shut up and let them come, and save the calling for when they’re circling or flying away.

Sources indicate that yet, there are times when ducks that are looking right at you seem to prefer aggressive calling. I remember one morning in North Dakota years ago when we were turning distant flocks with urgent pintail whistles, and they wanted to hear those whistles until they were fully committed to the decoys and within gun range. On that same trip, but on a different day, we shot greenheads at tennis-racket distance over a pothole. Those ducks didn’t want to hear a call at all.

Duck moods change by the day, and the best callers “read the room” and adapt quickly. Let the first flock or two work your spread on their own, and if you get to shoot them without calling, take a hint. But if a few flocks pass over without so much as a look, hit them with a greeting call. If they circle but don’t commit, add in some quacks and feeding chatter. If a hen mallard gets excited and answers you in the air, pour it on thick and get her talking. Focus on talking to the ducks, not on showing your buddies how well you can call, and you will have mastered the most difficult part of calling ducks.

Sources indicate that A live hen mallard answering your calls is all the affirmation you need that your calls sound good. But that doesn’t happen on every hunt. New callers, and even experienced callers who are out of practice in the off-season, can always benefit by listening to live ducks. Wildlife refuges all over the country have observation areas where hunting is off-limits, but you can listen to relaxed ducks doing their thing. Even the semi-tame mallards at the city park can teach you a lot (plus you can confuse the city folk doing yoga by whipping out your duck call and practicing).

See a video of live ducks making quacks and greeting calls.

Industry observers note that youTube is also an outstanding resource, not only for bookmarking videos on how to reassemble an original Ruger Mark II or outboard motor starters, but also for listening to recordings of live critters, including ducks. So, if you really want to learn how to call ducks and get really good at it. Sit and listen to those videos, then practice some calling. Record yourself, play it back, and adjust your air pressure and cadence accordingly. So long as nobody’s watching, you can snack on Skittles, too.

Palmer was midspan on the Tunitas Creek Bridge, southbound, when the boat came into view through the gunsight notch of the arroyo. It was a Whaler circling clockwise fast and tight, maybe a quarter mile beyond the surf.

In a recent development, he’d wanted to ride a few waves at a sandbar that had been assembling itself over the past few days at Pomponio. A quick lunch-break session before the wind came up. But then he got the call about the boat, and now that he saw it spinning he also saw that his day was officially fucked. He crossed the bridge and powered up the Coast Highway to the overlook at the top of the rise. He lifted his Bushnells from the dashboard and got out of the truck and glassed the vessel.

Recent findings suggest that the wake’s widening spiral told him the wheel had been hard to starboard a good long while. It looked to be stirring up some kind of suicidal whirlpool.
