⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, trail Runner managing editor Abby Levene caught up with cross-country skiing superstar Jessie Diggins in Kona, Hawaii, a few days before the Ironman World Championship.
  • After retiring from cross-country skiing as the most decorated American of all time, glide off into the sunset Jessie Diggins did not.
  • Sources indicate that diggins, 35, raced the Broken Arrow Triple Crown in June, as has become her annual ritual.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, trail Runner managing editor Abby Levene caught up with cross-country skiing superstar Jessie Diggins in Kona, Hawaii, a few days before the Ironman World Championship. In this exclusive interview, Diggins shares how she battled through a deep low to finish (and win) her first 100-miler, the lessons from cross-country skiing that she’s applying to trail running, and why she always puts on face glitter before a race.

After retiring from cross-country skiing as the most decorated American of all time, glide off into the sunset Jessie Diggins did not. The Olympic gold medalist earned one last piece of hardware in Milan-Cortina this spring—on bruised ribs no less—hung up the skis, and dove head-first into trail running.

Sources indicate that diggins, 35, raced the Broken Arrow Triple Crown in June, as has become her annual ritual. She then lined up against the world’s best trail runners at Sierre-Zinal in August, won the Superior 100-miler in September, and just last weekend won the (bear with me) Trail Animals Running Club Stone Cat Trail Festival 50-miler in Massachusetts.

Sources indicate that on paper, it’s been an effortless transition into a sport Diggins swears she is just doing for fun. But of course there is so much more to the story once you dig in. I was lucky enough to catch up with Diggins at the epicenter of yet another endurance sport—the Ironman World Championship—in Kona, Hawaii, last month. She’d just come from a snorkeling expedition trying to find a sea turtle. (So far no luck.) Gazing out onto the turquoise waves crashing into shore, we chatted about what she’s learned and loved about trail running so far. That list includes (and is not limited to) how trail running really is a team sport, achieving personal goals is bigger than the results, fueling on a “washing machine” stomach is not easy, and the power of glitter translates from snowy trails to dry ones.

This interview has been edited for clarity. You can also watch some of it above.

Sources indicate that jessie: It was a really cool experience. It was so humbling, but so exciting to tackle a totally different challenge. I was filled with curiosity: What will this feel like? What’s going to happen to my body? What will happen inside my brain? How does this work?

Recent findings suggest that having a crew and pacers like that is very different from skiing. [In skiing] you are alone on the trail, and people can cheer for you, but you don’t actually have anyone with you on the trail. And so it was just so exciting I got to do it with a team. That was really significant for me. I’m a very team-oriented person, and I would get so excited to come into the aid station and see the crew and to get to have a pacer with me. Even when I was falling apart and couldn’t even  talk—I was at a really low point—it was just like, ‘I’m here with my team and I’m pushing my limits and I’m seeing what’s possible for me.’ And that’s so exciting.

It has been revealed that I would just tell myself ‘every step you take is a step you don’t have to take again.’ So I was just like, ‘I’m doing it. I’m slowly working towards that finish line, step by step.’ It was so funny because even when I was deeply uncomfortable, I never actually thought about quitting, which I thought I would. It was more just like I’m so uncomfortable, but I know I can if I just keep moving. Even if I’m slowing down, even if I’m not even able to run, I have to just power hike this section. I’m still moving towards my goal. I’m in the process of getting there, and that’s exciting in and of itself.

I kind of wanted to set up a charcuterie board of the trail world and try different things because they were all so different, right? Broken Arrow is a huge festival and it was a multi-day thing, so oh my gosh, what is day three gonna feel like? Can I even run downhill on day three?

And then Sierre-Zinal is so historic, and it was such a cool course. It was beautiful, and it was like experiencing a very classic “short” trail race, right? I was like, ‘this is not short.’ It took me 3 hours, but it was so cool to experience.

It has been revealed that and then going into the 100 miler, it was different and more of a backyard format. Or not a backyard in terms of the laps, but like there was no award ceremony. It wasn’t about winning. It was just about doing it, and I love that. That is so aligned with how I feel about racing. It’s like, ‘No, we don’t really care who wins. We just want everyone to challenge themselves and hopefully make their goal of crossing the finish line.’ And that was so cool for me.

It has been revealed that and so getting to be a part of each of these events, I got to experience so many different angles of the trail world and meet so many people. And for me, that was a major thing, too: feeling the sense of community that was around every single race and making newly introduced friends and trying something new. That was very cool.

No, I definitely am excited to do more. I don’t know what that’s gonna look like yet, but I feel like just getting to be involved in this world is so cool and so exciting. So, I’m sort of now in the phase of like, ‘OK, I feel like I’m bouncing back with 100. Like, my body’s coming back, and now I can start dreaming and scheming and brainstorming, like what else do I want to do? What else is out there? What excites me? What feels like the appropriate challenge for this phase of my life?’ Yeah, I’m trying to figure it all out.

Recent findings suggest that I think the biggest thing was in training, like listening to my body. So I stopped wearing a heart rate monitor like five or six years ago, and it was really about being in tune and listening to my body and figuring out where I can push. What does it feel like when I’m riding that line of level three, and what are the signals in my body when I’ve gone over that line and I need to pull it back?

And so really trying to deeply understand how I feel, and I feel like that’s helped me steer away from injuries too, because I’m not relying on metrics. I want to feel how my body feels and respond to that and act on those feelings.I think that’s something I’m taking with me because I’m well aware now that running can really beat you up in a different way. Even listening to my body and learning how much can I eat while I’m running because your stomach is a washing machine and that does not happen in cross-country skiing.

In a recent development, I think it was really exciting in my final years of cross-country skiing, learning more about high-carb fueling and having all these great products come on board. Because in a ski race, let’s say a 50-kilometer race, you come through a feed zone, but you have gloves and your hands are in poles, so you are not like ripping open a gel. You’ll end up stabbing yourself in the face. And so what you do is you tuck your poles under your armpits and you grab the feed bottle, which is usually an actual baby bottle with the lid taken off, from a coach who cannot run with you, they have to just stand there and hold it by the rim. So you grab it while you are gliding quite quickly. You down it so you get like a few good sips, and then you have to chuck the bottle on the side and keep moving. And so having really high carb drink mixes where you can, if you only can get a few mouthfuls, you need them to count, and so having these was huge. Because before it’d be like, ‘I guess we’ll boil down Coke to de-fizz it, and that’s what you can have.’ But it  just wasn’t high carb enough, and the electrolyte balance might not have been great.

Now there’s so many options, and that really changed the way I could race. And so now, in trail racing, there’s all these different gels. You can find the one that works for you. There’s all these different mixes. You can find the amount of salt that works for you. That’s been really cool. Being able to tailor it. I feel like 15 years ago, there weren’t that many options. Now having more options is power.

Recent findings suggest that I do get scared. It’s funny. I just saw on the elevator this morning a woman was wearing glitter, and I was like, ‘Yes!’ That was my whole thing through my ski career. And it came out of being scared and being nervous. And I feel like people don’t always know that that’s the origin. But I would get so nervous for races, and a little bit of nerves is great. It means you care. If you’re not nervous for a race, it’s sort of like, ‘Why am I doing this?’ You know, then it’s time to maybe examine, do I really care about what I’m doing?

At the end of the day, yes, there’s a lot of pressure. There can be expectations. There can be a lot of lights. A lot of people are watching you, but you get to do this. You get to challenge yourself and see what’s possible. And that, in and of itself, is such an amazing opportunity.

Latest Update: The Hunt for the Jameson Buck, a 250-Inch Kansas Legend That Lived in an Old Strip Mine

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, this story, “Ghost Buck,” appeared in the November 1991 problem of Outdoor Life.
  • Recent findings suggest that the massive whitetail moved steadily, head lowered, nosing a course through a lunarlike landscape of earth mounds, dark puddles and hair-thick brush.
  • Then abruptly the buck froze, as if gripped by an old instinct for caution.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, this story, “Ghost Buck,” appeared in the November 1991 problem of Outdoor Life. The Bruce Jameson buck ultimately scored 248 1/8 inches after deductions, according to Boone and Crockett. Although it was one of the top-scoring archery bucks of all time when it was killed, it’s listed as the 16th largest nontypical ever taken in Kansas. Though the story mentions Pope and Young, Jameson’s name isn’t listed among its records. The rack is now owned by Bass Pro Shops.

Recent findings suggest that the massive whitetail moved steadily, head lowered, nosing a course through a lunarlike landscape of earth mounds, dark puddles and hair-thick brush. Strip mining had turned the area raw and made hunting supremely difficult. Yet this giant of a buck moved on. Something compelled him, an urge perhaps. It was mid-November, the peak of the rut.

Then abruptly the buck froze, as if gripped by an old instinct for caution. From atop a rise, he surveyed the area.

Industry observers note that to bowhunter Bruce Jameson, who knelt against the base of a cottonwood 50 yards away, it was now clear that all of the speculation about the buck had been true. Somehow the hundreds of hunters before him who had failed to get a close look at this ghost buck had emerged with an accurate picture — perhaps because it was nearly impossible to exaggerate in describing the animal. Everything about the buck was massive. His long, heavy body seemed to melt into a neck that was a barrel of solid muscle from supporting his towering, forearm-thick antlers. The bowhunter clutched his compound Pearson Spoiler and saw his knuckles turn a splotchy white.

This buck, so well-known but seldom seen, had drawn Jameson into the woods 20 of the past 21 mornings. He had been taunted by a combination of too much distance and brush. Day after day, there had been no clear shot. Still, the bowhunter felt a kind of jubila­tion as he watched the world-class whitetail lower his head and fade into the brush. After all, he had just accomplished something no other hunter had — he had seen the ghost buck while hunting.

According to recent reports, at the time, the walls of Jameson’s Pittsburg, Kan­sas, bowhunting and taxidermy shop were lined with big-game mounts. Most were whitetail bucks of envi­able size. Still, to a mount, they were overshadowed by one buck in particular, which, once noticed, instantly took your eyes away from the rest. Hunters had come from all parts of southeastern Kansas to marvel at this huge non-typical buck. His main beams were nearly as thick as a softball where they rose from the mount, and they thickened as they climbed into a crown of spike­ like points. When displayed at a trophy deer show, people had crowded around, labeling it the most im­pressive non-typical to come from a state that’s been dominating the record books for a quarter-century.

It has been revealed that equally provocative was the fact that the deer was still in the wild. The display cape was that of another buck. The gargantuan antlers had been found after the ghost buck had shed them the previous winter. It wasn’t the first time, either.

Deer hunters around town got their first hint of an exceptional horned buck when John Jameson, Bruce’s father, happened upon a shed antler during a 1987 bowhunt. Though bleached from the sun and pocked by rodents, there was no mistaking that it came from a trophy buck. The single antler was unusually massive and sported eight points.

According to recent reports, local hunters were surprised that no one had ever seen the buck that carried it. Many speculated that the beast had already died a natural death. The following spring though, Jameson’s nephew, Doug Kratz, discovered that the ghost was still in their presence when he happened across a massive, freshly shed antler. A few weeks later the other side, an eye­ opening set, also turned up. Together the two antlers carried a total of 22 points.

The presence of the big buck in the Pittsburg area was particularly exciting to the Jamesons. Bruce Jameson is one of 10 children who grew up hunting and fishing with their father. In fact, all of the Jamesons, including their father, still bow hunt together regularly. Yet, the Jameson’s home range, southeastern Kansas, is the only area of the state not known for producing exceptional whitetail racks. Hunting pressure is high and the habitat fair at best for producing big bucks.

Industry observers note that like scores of other hunters, Jameson planned on hunting the ghost buck hard during the 1988 season, but his upcoming taxidermy and bowhunting shop was gaining popularity with local hunters. He couldn’t get away.

In a recent development, jameson was determined, however, to keep his ears open while he manned his Main Street shop. The progressing season started out as a repeat of the past: no sightings, and no signs of a huge whitetail — no big tracks, massive rubs or huge scrapes. Still, the attraction of this buck, and his mystique, seemed to build with each passing week.

There probably isn’t a deer camp or small hunting town in America that doesn’t have a legendary buck — an animal so massive, so elu­sive, so remarked upon, that his image is forever associated with something beyond the ordinary. The ghost buck is an idea more than a form, and as such, it has a special invincibil­ity. Yet Bruce Jameson was determined to change that.

In a recent development, luck helped. Soon, Jameson’s good friend Dennis Scales accomplished something that instantly made him a local celebrity — he glimpsed the ghost buck. It was still early in the morning when Stales spotted a doe and a small buck feeding across a field of milo stubble.

From his truck, Scales could easily watch as the unimpressive pair fed across the expanse of knee-high cover. Then it happened. Scales, an avid deer hunter, watched in wonder as the big non-typical rose from the scant cover and hurried toward the little buck and doe. As soon as the monster buck reached the doe he in­stantly flattened out, totally out of sight in what looked like open cover. It was a ritual that Scales witnessed three times before the passing of a distant pickup truck spooked the big whitetail into the woods. No one else saw the famous buck during the gun or bow season.

Recent findings suggest that those who’ve driven the southeastern Kansas area can understand the amazement sur­rounding the notion of a giant buck in flatlands country. With a decided absence of wilder­ ness, every mile of land is evenly gridded by gravel roads that are often traveled by small­ game hunters and fishermen, farmers and com­muters.

Recent findings suggest that despite Scales’ sighting, and the discovery of another huge shed antler, Jameson was not encouraged. “My heart would start pounding when I would look up and think of myself in a tree with him coming down the trail,” he mused. “But I knew it was going to be tough to pick one buck, a buck that you know is at least 5 1/2 years old, in an area with heavy pressure and heavy cover. I also knew that I’d hunted this area all of my life and never seen the buck. I couldn’t help but occasionally wonder if he was still alive.”.

One summer evening, Jameson found out. “I do quite a bit of looking in August,” he mentioned. “The bucks will be hanging together, and because they haven’t been pressured you can sometimes catch them coming out to feed in the evenings.”.

It has been revealed that along with a cousin, Bruce drove to a soybean field in his hunting area. Most sum­mertime bucks are calm and tolerant of distant vehicles, but one buck in particular melted into the nearby woods when Jameson was still 150 yards away. That was close enough.

“I didn’t need binoculars to know it was him,” Jameson recalled. “I was in a state of awe. I just turned to my cousin and remarked, ‘You have no idea what you just saw — he’s one of the best in the state, probably one of the best in the nation.’ It was good to know that I’d at least get a chance to hunt him.”.

Jameson also knew that he wouldn’t be alone in his quest. The lad who’d found the most recent sheds had disclosed the buck’s location. Going into the season about a dozen bowhunters had sworn to hold out for this buck, which seemed now more flesh than ghost. In the weeks before the opening of deer season, a continuous cloud of dust hung over the dirt roads as hunters and non-hunters alike cruised along, hoping for a glimpse of the legendary buck. Then on October 1, bowhunters swarmed into the woods, but again it was as if the buck had turned to mist.

Meanwhile, Jameson bided his time, hop­ing the upcoming rut would draw the buck out. Though Jameson had a good idea where the deer lived, he couldn’t get permission to enter the property. Instead, he set up 1 1/2 miles away and waited.

Industry observers note that “I figured that once the rut started he’d start covering more ground,” Jameson rea­soned. “Even then I knew he’d be tough be­ cause of the terrain.”.

Industry observers note that deer hunting in this part of Kansas can be, well, the pits. This is coal country. In previous decades huge chunks of ground were clawed open to get at coal deposits. The strip-mined areas look like moon surface.

Industry observers note that piles of dirt from eight to 30 feet high lay interspaced with water-filled pits. Where there is dirt there is dense brush. The jungle — and swamplike strip pits offer some of the most difficult hunting in the nation.

Sources indicate that jameson spent his first week in a tree at the edge of “the pits” near a slough that would offer the buck the easiest and most direct route through the area. He saw only a small buck and some fawns.

Frustrated, he moved to an area that held a small green wheat field and a scattering of hedge trees. Though he sighted and passed up a number of lesser bucks, there was no sign of the ghost buck. The unseasonably warm and dry weather that ushered in the November rut­ — hunters in the area saw more mosquitoes than snowflakes — further tilted the odds against Jameson.

It has been revealed that finally, Jameson got a much needed break in the form of a light shower, which would allow him to pick up tracks. He started slowly traveling the back roads.

It has been revealed that “We often look for what we call ‘shortcut’ trails in the dust on the shoulders of roads,” Jameson explained. “They’re basically trails that major bucks use to cover a lot of ground and to get from section to section without being seen.”.

The veteran hunter observed that these shortcut trails seem to be utilized only by big bucks, seldom by does or lesser bucks. “You’ll usually only find the tracks of one or two bucks,” Jameson added. “We check the road edges because the trails are tough to see or follow in the woods, they get used so little.”.

A few years earlier, in just such a place, one of his brothers had arrowed a trophy with a Boone and Crockett Club non-typical score in excess of 200 points.

Jameson soon found tracks coming and going from the section he’d hunted earlier in the season. There were two sets of buck tracks: one significant, the other less so. Experience told the hunter that the larger set probably belonged to a dark-racked buck he’d seen and passed up near the wheat field.

Industry observers note that but what about the other tracks? They weren’t overly impressive, and he couldn’t remember seeing them before. But it was their location, not their size, that excited Jameson. It was a prime spot for an old, wary buck to travel. “Maybe,” he thought, “just maybe …”.

Fired by a hunch, Jameson took a rare morning off from his treestand vigil and planned to move from his wheat field location to the slough at the edge of the pits where he’d first started.

Jameson had just started the walk into the slough when something caught his eye. “I looked across the field and there he was,” said Jameson. “I could tell it was him no problem. He had his nose down bird-dogging it back and forth. He was looking for a doe.”.

It has been revealed that jameson’s hunch was confirmed; the buck had gone right through the slough where he’d wanted his stand. But rather than bemoan his bad timing, Jameson decided to make the best of the situation as he watched the non-typical disappear into the timber.

“A lot of hunters make the mistake of seeing a big buck and then not doing anything about it,” noted Jameson. “We’ve taken sev­eral trophy-class bucks by swinging around and getting ahead of them. Sometimes it works, sometimes it doesn’t, but I figured it was worth a try.”.

In a recent development, the buck had been heading north, possibly toward the shortcut trail Jameson had found a few days earlier. The bowhunter wasted no time circling ahead of the buck. He ran down the trail that bisected the two sections, jumped a fence, and sprinted to the top of one of the many dirt mounds.

Recent findings suggest that it was a guess — hoping the buck would cross 30 yards to his right — but it was Jameson’s only chance. Even if the buck came his way he knew that the thick underbrush would make a shot next to impossible.

Jameson had been in place only five min­utes when he caught movement. It was the ghost buck, passing at a steady clip. The range was too long and the brush too thick. Jameson’s heart was drumming against his rib cage. He tried to sneak a few steps closer. but he couldn’t get within 50 yards.

Then, for reasons unclear to the hunter. the whitetail suddenly stopped and raised his head. In the next moment, he was gone. disappearing over the edge of a mound. Jameson found himself staring at the scene as it was just minutes ago — that is, without the ghost buck­ — and he felt a kind of pleasurable sadness. “It was a strange feeling.” he remembered. “I’d actually figured out where he’d go, but I was also disappointed. You simply don’t get many chances at a deer like him. He sure had proven that over the past several seasons. I had to wonder whether I’d ever get another chance.”.

It has been revealed that feeling almost electrified, Jameson waited a few minutes before sneaking back carefully to the spot where he”d last seen the whitetail. At least, he reasoned, he could get a look at the tracks and perhaps figure out once again where the buck was heading.

Recent findings suggest that when he saw them, he instantly recognized the tracks — they were the smaller set he’d seen on the shortcut trail. Jameson walked in the direction the buck had taken and paused at the top of the next mound, wondering why he hadn’t seen the deer cresting one of the sea of little ridges.

In a recent development, without warning, there was a loud crash. Jameson twisted around and saw the buck of his dreams jump from a hiding place 35 yards away, staying to a course that kept distance between him and the bowhunter. Instinct took over. It seemed Jameson’s hundreds of hours of indoor and outdoor shooting had somehow led him to this shot — he was ready. “I drew, got ahead of the buck, and when the time was right, I released the arrow without actually thinking about it.”.

It has been revealed that jameson watched his Anderson 365 mag­num broadhead enter the buck as the animal stepped through a tiny clearing. Ironically. it was one of the rare occasions when this sharp­ shooting bowhunter had been unsure of his arrow placement. He watched the buck pause briefly atop the next mound, then move out of sight as if not seriously wounded.

At the thought of a bad hit on such a magnificent animal, Jameson fell to his knees and was sick. Long a man of deep conviction, he did what came naturally in a time of crisis — he mentioned a quick prayer for the animal’s fast and humane death. “I call upon God anytime I feel I need help.” he said. Then he thought to go get his father, who was waiting nearby.

An hour later Jameson, his father, John, and his brother Richard were back in the area. The trio quietly surveyed the scene of the shot. There was blood. They soon found the arrow. but it was floating in a nearby pit of water, wave-cleansed of any tissue or hair.

It has been revealed that after deciding the trail looked good, the trio inched in the direction the ghost buck had taken. They saw that the buck had stopped and changed directions. The father and sons found the huge whitetail at the top of the next dump­ — barely 70 yards away from where it had been hit. Clearly, the ghost buck had succumbed within a matter of a few seconds.

Sources indicate that “When he saw the deer,” Jameson re­called of his father, “tears came to his eyes and he hugged me around the neck. He’s always had a great sense of pride in each of his six sons and our accomplishments. I’ll never forget it.”.

Recent findings suggest that what will forever be known as the “Jameson buck” will go down as one of the most impres­sive whitetail bucks of all time. The mass of the rack was almost indescribable and, along with the skull plate, weighed an eye-opening 12 pounds.

In a recent development, after the 60-day drying period, the mam­moth rack scored 253 6/8 Pope and Young Club points — the tally may well go higher when scored by the club’s official panel. As it stands, the “Jameson buck” is the third largest non­ typical whitetail arrowed in history.

Read Next: I Shot the Third Biggest Elk of All Time.

It has been revealed that A close look at the ghost buck revealed how he had lived virtually undetected by sportsmen for years. Though he field-dressed at 243 pounds, his feet sported surprisingly small hoofs. Jameson also theorized that the jungle of points on the buck’s rack may have kept him from rubbing on big trees. “When you really start looking at the rack you realize that he couldn’t rub all of his velvet on a big tree,” said the hunter. “He probably had to rely on small trees or maybe even brush. It’s possible we saw his rubs and just dismissed them as those of a small buck.”.

#91129. 5 Steps To Taking An Elk With An Over-The-Counter Tag

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2131 w)

5 Steps To Taking An Elk With An Over-The-Counter Tag

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2131 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fieldandstream

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Over-the-counter (OTC) elk units tend to get a bad rap.
  • Sources indicate that the good news: OTC units can produce incredible hunting for elk if you follow these guidelines.
  • In a recent development, locating OTC elk units, thanks to newly polished western game and fish websites, is a breeze.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over-the-counter (OTC) elk units tend to get a bad rap. It doesn’t matter, either, if the particular unit boasts unlimited tags or those offered on a first-come basis. Most hunters will be quick to sneer at them. Of course, hunting pressure in OTC units is going to be higher than those found in coveted draw units. Elk encounters may be fewer, and made-by-elk vocalizations may be hard to come by. However, if the thought of going years (sometimes decades) in between guttural bugles and basins littered with golden aspens disgusts you, OTC units need to become your best friend. Successful OTC elk hunting, whether you’re toting a bow or rifle, comes down to having a system for success. The following advice applies to both crowds. If you put it to practice, a date with an OTC bull is likely in the coming weeks and months.

Sources indicate that the good news: OTC units can produce incredible hunting for elk if you follow these guidelines. Forget the odds and the naysayers. If you’re willing to work hard and be relentless, good things will happen. Colorado boasts the world’s largest elk population (just north of 280,000 animals) and gives resident and nonresident bowhunters a total of 137 out of 184 units to chase their OTC elk dreams in—we are going to refer to it often.

In a recent development, locating OTC elk units, thanks to newly polished western game and fish websites, is a breeze. Idaho, for instance, provides OTC tags on a first-come basis in all but one of its elk management zones and all but three of its elk management units. Naturally, popular units go fast, so do your research and be ready to go when those units go on sale. Colorado, on the other hand, offers unlimited tags in its OTC units, and tags can be purchased starting in early August through the end of the season. Colorado’s OTC units are easily discovered by simply looking at the regulation’s brochure. These units are highlighted and clearly marked.

When looking for a prospective OTC elk unit, the first thing I like to do is check out hunter success. Yes, I realize these percentage rates are often skewed due to bowhunters who don’t hunt at all, hunt only a day or two, or never leave the comfort of their Chevy, however, I do believe they have a lot of value. If you can locate a hunt unit or better yet a trio or more that have connecting borders that boast success rates above 10 percent, they are worth a look. Most western states ask hunters to fill out surveys at the end of the season, and results are then posted to the state’s game and fish website. Take advantage. While you’re looking at success rates, it’s also a good idea to peek at recent population counts and bull-to-cow ratios. Again, most every western state will have this information on their website. I like to print out success rates, population, and bull-to-cow ratio sheets and use them to triangulate a likely hunt unit.

Sources indicate that don’t disregard isolated single units either, especially if they border draw units. I’ve had some great hunts pressing in close to a draw-unit area and hunting the border. The biggest reason I like connecting units is if I’m struggling to find elk, I don’t like to wait around. Elk are major travelers. If I spend a full day hunting an area and don’t see a single elk, hear a bugle or at the very least see some greasy sign, I bounce. If you do opt to put all of your OTC eggs into a single unit, be sure that unit has plenty of National Forest and BLM access, which takes us to Step 2.

Recent findings suggest that now that you have a few units in mind, it’s time to pull those units up on your onX Hunt App. If you don’t have onX, get it. Not only does this digital mapping system allow you to mark likely hunt locales, but it also reveals public/private land boundaries and is loaded with an abundance of other helpful features like hunt unit boundaries and the like.

What are you looking for? Access for starters. I like to locate off-the-beaten-path areas that require a mile or more jaunt to get into them and are restricted to travel on foot, horseback, or pedal power. If you can locate a trail snaking through vast acres of public land with no other road access available for miles around, take note of it. In addition to locating off-the-beaten-path locations, you’ll also want to mark between eight and 10 (the more, the better) right-off-the-road areas. No, I’m not crazy. The go-deep drum has been beaten hard, which has increased competition in the backcountry and left piles of easy-access spots abandoned. Locate areas right off of a main road that dive into a hellish bottom or require a long, vertical walk. Both will discourage the masses. A pair of my hunting partners have utilized this off-the-road tactic over the past two seasons in Colorado. The results have been four public-land bulls over a total of 10 hunt days, and my amigos slept in the comfort of their camper each night.

In a recent development, it’s also a good idea, especially once you’ve decided on a hunt unit, to get a good paper topo map. I prefer those from HuntData due to the fact that they are printed on Dura-Map fabric, which stands up against weather and in-and-out-of-pack abuse.

With your hunt area pulled up on onX maps and your paper map in hand, it’s time to look for likely elk haunts. If the plan is to pack in deep and seek secluded areas, remember that elk need water, cover, and food. The more rugged the country, the better. Any areas with deep drainages lined by steep slopes should be noted. These drainages offer thick bedding cover, and streams often trickle down their middles. Other areas of interest should be steep country that levels out on large benches (long, flat spots amidst steep country) before dropping off once again. Elk love to rut on benches. Other notable spots include small, secluded meadows in the middle of a sea of deep, dark timber. Elk will feed in these meadows early and late, and most will contain at least one well-used wallow.

Sources indicate that if your destination is Colorado, don’t overlook units with wilderness areas inside their boundaries. In Colorado, both residents and non-residents can access wilderness areas without a guide, and these locations are usually the best recipe for getting away from people and experiencing a true backcountry hunt. Travel into wilderness areas is limited to foot and horseback only. Simplify your OTC unit/wilderness area search by visiting coloradowilderness.com.

Read Next: Elk Hunting Archery Tactics for Post-Rut Bulls.

Sources indicate that what about north-facing slopes? Sure, north-facing slopes are good for bedding, but over the years, especially during the rut, I don’t worry at all about which direction a slope faces. I go where the elk are.

If you like the dive-off-the-road strategy or want to use it as a backup if your go-deep idea goes to crap, again, look for areas that drop rapidly in elevation. Elk will hold up in deep dark holes. Another option, and one my hunting partners and I use a lot, is the straight-up approach. If you can find some off-the-road vert that leads to a good bench, mark it. The more spots you have marked, the more you can bounce in and out of. Another great tactic is to look at easy-access areas that will draw the masses, and then located the nastiest, steepest area in close proximity to these areas. These locations will often fill up with pressured elk. Remember, it takes only one bull to cooperate.

Recent findings suggest that I know it’s been written about more times than Gene Simmons has flicked his tongue at Kiss concert, but it’s really a must do. Call the local state game and fish office nearest your hunt locale and get the number for the area biologist. I love these folks. Why? Simple, they spend most all of their time in the field compiling data, and most everyone of them I’ve ever talked to is dying to share it with a source other than a spreadsheet.

The trick is to honor their time. If you’re lucky enough to get them on the phone, have a list of pre-prepared questions written down. They will appreciate this and will be more apt to provide helpful information. Chances are, however, you won’t get them on the phone. No biggie. Leave a message and they will call you back. The problem is they will call you back while you’re checking out of the grocery store or at some other inopportune time—mark my words. For this reason, I carry my list of questions in my wallet. This way I have my questions on-hand at all times. Here is a quick list to get you started. Feel free to add your own.

Recent findings suggest that these are the areas I’m looking at. Can you recommend any others where I may be able to get away from people and find elk?

Have there been any winter mortality challenges or any other factors in the area that have led to a recent population decline?

Are there any special camping or hunting rules in this location that I need to be aware of?

How have calf survival rates been over the past few years?

Is there anything you know of that should discourage me from hunting this area?

From a biologist’s point of view, what about any encouraging factors?

Sadly, it’s this step that most don’t complete—and those that do won’t follow the advice to come. You’ve done the research and are all ready to go, so, please, go! Many would-be elk hunters, after they’ve done all the leg work, simply don’t go. They talk themselves out of the idea and listen to reports from naysayers who’ve had “bad” OTC experiences. Remember, most of these experiences were the sole fault of the participant. I had a guy tell me last year at a sporting goods store that he hadn’t heard a bugle in 10 days of hunting. He was hunting the same general area my hunting partners and I were, and we’d heard multiple bugles each day and killed a pair of bulls. The difference: He expected the unit to be like an elk hunting video. He was driving access roads and trying to solicit bugles from his truck. This leads us into the second half of Step 5.

It has been revealed that it’s essential that you go into your hunt with realistic expectations. Unless you end up on a bench with a handful of hot cows and a number of satellite bulls circling the girls with herd bull trying to protect his harem, it’s likely you won’t hear the type of bugling you’ll see on outdoor television. Remember, you’re hunting pressured land and elk that have likely been called to. Lots of bulls come in silent to bull and cow talk.

Another key tip (especially if this is your maiden voyage into the elk woods) is to have realistic expectations when it comes to the size of your harvest. I live in Colorado, and unless I have a draw tag in my pocket, I shoot the first legal bull I see. This takes the pressure off and typically allows me to fill my freezer with meat. Most Colorado OTC units offer either-sex licenses, and there have been many seasons where I slammed a broadhead-tipped arrow through a tasty cow.

Go into the hunt with the mindset that you will shoot the first legal elk you’ll see, and it will be that much more enjoyable. I also recommend, especially if this is your first trip into an area, to simply focus your hunt around learning your unit. Learn and take note of your access points. Keep notes about elk encounters and the like. The goal is just to get into elk. If you find a place void of people and teeming with elk, you’ve found a gem you can go back to on those years you don’t have a draw tag in your wallet.

With seasons open across the West, Colorado may be your best option. When it comes to a few units to help jumpstart your search, look to those in the states Northwest and Southwest. A few with connecting borders include 11, 21, and 22 as well as 80, 81, and 78.

It has been revealed that there you have it. All the info you need to go OTC. Get after it!

Send messages and get location check-ins without cell service, reach the Garmin Response coordination center for 24/7 help, and let friends and family know where you are with location sharing. And of course, it’s got all the bells and whistles of a top-tier GPS watch, including 78 hours of battery life in GPS mode. Plus with an AMOLED Sapphire face it’s basically indestructible. If you’ve been eyeing this bad boy now is the time to send it.

In a recent development, I live in these Smartwool Performance socks during winter, both on the run and in daily life. That’s because they are super warm but also pretty thin. In other words, I can wear my normal shoe size without squeezing my toes. Bonus points for fun patterns.

I’ve been using an older version of this pillow for years and can confidently say whether you’re fastpacking or simply want to sleep better when you’re traveling, this Sea to Summit Aeros Premium Pillow will revolutionize your life. #91125. Is Early-Season Skiing Worth It? Here’s the Case for Going.

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (578 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Skimag ↗ Open Full Page

Is Early-Season Skiing Worth It? Here’s the Case for Going.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (578 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Skimag

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There’s a lot to love about skiing: being outdoors, pushing yourself to improve, finding your flow, and being part of ski culture.
  • Industry observers note that the solution is early-season skiing.
  • Plus, everything that makes skiing great still stands: you’re outside, you’re improving, you’re dipping into your flow state, and you’re more a part of ski culture than if you were to come for President’s Weekend like everyone else.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Courtesy of Vail Resorts).

There’s a lot to love about skiing: being outdoors, pushing yourself to improve, finding your flow, and being part of ski culture. But too often, the things that make skiing great get overshadowed by cost and crowds. It’s hard to find your flow when the run is crowded, and even the best ski day is hard to enjoy when lodging, lift tickets, and lunch leave you financially stretched.

Industry observers note that the solution is early-season skiing. Few people book a ski trip in November or early December, and even local skiers tend to be unenthused. But I think they’re missing out. In fact, early season is one of my favorite times to ski. Early season turns have led to breakthroughs in my technique, and it’s one of the only times when the mountain feels small enough to meet up with friends.

Plus, everything that makes skiing great still stands: you’re outside, you’re improving, you’re dipping into your flow state, and you’re more a part of ski culture than if you were to come for President’s Weekend like everyone else.

And the things that make skiing less appealing are non-challenges.

According to recent reports, the cost of an early ski season trip can be half or even a third of what you’ll pay just a few weeks later. In Jackson Hole, for example, if you visit in early December, rather than Christmas week, you’ll pay $85 for a lift ticket instead of $340. Similarly, a room at the ultra-luxe slopeside Hotel Terra Jackson Hole increases by $600 a night based on whether you stay in early or late December. The same goes for big ski weeks like spring break and Presidents’ Day—and the weeks in between aren’t much cheaper.

And then there’s the fact that when you’re not skiing at the same time as everyone else, every aspect of the day (or your entire trip) becomes more enjoyable. You’ll get in more skiing thanks to shorter (or nonexistent) lift lines, and you don’t have to worry about running into someone on the way down. And when you aren’t one of 10 people waiting in line for rental gear or a table at the restaurant, you’ll get warmer, more personalized service. (Plus, in early season, everyone is fresh and excited for the season ahead, not tired and over it.).

When the mountain is fully open, and everyone’s ski legs are firing, the pressure to go major is real. It can be difficult and dangerous to try to keep up, especially if you’re fresh to skiing or it’s your first (or only) ski trip of the year.

It has been revealed that but in the early season, everyone is still getting their ski legs under them, and the skiing is more about fine-tuning your technique and rebuilding muscle. There’s nothing showy about it, and most people leave their egos at home.

The biggest argument against early season skiing is the lack of snow. Indeed, in the early season, the snow hasn’t had time to accumulate. Often, only the lower parts of the mountain are open, and sometimes only thanks to snowmaking. It’s not the time to do a hike-to, and you’ll rarely find any powder, so show up with your expectations (and ego) in check.

But if you’re willing to rethink what a ski day should look like, you can enjoy everything that makes skiing great while avoiding its biggest drawbacks.

  • “She was an exceptional climbing guide and human being,” Apex Adventure Alliance wrote in a statement to Outside.
  • It has been revealed that originally from Duluth, Minnesota, Pelosi had long structured her life around her various passions: snowboarding, cycling, and, eventually, an all-encompassing love of climbing and the community around it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Courtesy of Michael Hall).

Audrie Pelosi found climbing after moving to Baraboo, Wisconsin. It wasn’t long before the quartzite cliffs of Devil’s Lake became a cornerstone of her life. She climbed there, worked there, and eventually became its steward as a guide with Apex Adventure Alliance (AAA), bringing newly introduced climbers to the same arena in which she’d begun.

“She was an exceptional climbing guide and human being,” Apex Adventure Alliance wrote in a statement to Outside. “She was a force in our community and at our guide service. We all will miss her dearly.”.

It has been revealed that originally from Duluth, Minnesota, Pelosi had long structured her life around her various passions: snowboarding, cycling, and, eventually, an all-encompassing love of climbing and the community around it. Her passion radiated outwards: she volunteered locally and, in 2026, ran for a Wisconsin Climbers Association board seat, hoping to become more involved in stewardship and community building. “I believe in showing up, doing the work, and listening to the community,” Pelosi wrote in her candidate statement.

“With her friends and community, Audrie was so generous,” said Garrett Hopkins, AAA’s owner. “That generosity flowed into her climbing, biking, and snowboarding too. When I was living on the road, I knew her couch was always open for a spot to crash if my van was being repaired. She spent countless hours with young climbers in an effort to elevate the safety of the next generation coming up.”.

Pelosi met her husband, Jimmy “The Fox” Robinson, at a snowboard event at Welch Village, Minnesota, and in 2023 the two married atop Mount Bohemia (1,465ft) on Lake Superior. From then on, Pelosi had the nickname “Mrs. The Fox.” One of her friends, Anastasia Exterovich, set up a GoFundMe to raise money for Pelosi’s family in the wake of her passing. She called the pair the “raddest couple.”.

“In my last conversation with Audrie, she joked about selling her handmade bike chain link earrings to anyone who wanted them for ‘free.99,’” Exterovich wrote. “It was such a simple statement made in passing, but it perfectly encapsulated who she was as a person. Even when she didn’t have much, she would give things away freely without hesitation, whether that was earrings, a smile, a laugh, a quick bike tune-up, or a belay.”.

Pelosi passed on May 30, 2026 working as a guide at  Devil’s Lake State Park, teaching a climbing course near the park’s East Bluff. During the course, Pelosi fell from the bluff and suffered fatal injuries. She is survived by her husband, her family, and the broader climbing community in Wisconsin.

Colorado Trail and Continental Divide Trail ‘Extensively Damaged’ After Severe Flooding: Here’s What We Know

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (872 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This article was updated on November 18, 2026, at 11:48 a.m.
  • Sources indicate that in just over a week, two massive flooding events hit southwestern Colorado, destroying homes, businesses, and infrastructure across numerous mountain towns.
  • “Rebuilding these damaged sections will not be quick, easy, or cheap,” Paul Talley, executive director of the Colorado Trail Foundation (CTF), said in a November 5 revision on the floods.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This article was updated on November 18, 2026, at 11:48 a.m. with additional information regarding the condition of the Colorado Trail section 28 and the Continental Divide Trail.

Sources indicate that in just over a week, two massive flooding events hit southwestern Colorado, destroying homes, businesses, and infrastructure across numerous mountain towns. But property is not all that the floods affected. Parts of both the Continental Divide Trail (CDT) and the Colorado Trail (CT) suffered damage that locals and trail organizations are calling “extensive” and “severe”, and which could take a very long time to repair.

“Rebuilding these damaged sections will not be quick, easy, or cheap,” Paul Talley, executive director of the Colorado Trail Foundation (CTF), said in a November 5 revision on the floods. “But we are committed to rebuilding.”.

It has been revealed that as many of these areas are still inaccessible, there is very little confirmed information on their current state. Videos circulating online show missing bridges at key river crossings, and reports from the USFS and other agencies indicate that trailheads are damaged, and “heavy debris” is blocking some sections. But there has yet to be a full, official report on damage to these trails.

Here is what we know so far based on official updates, local reports, and videos.

It has been revealed that junction Creek is the CT’s southernmost section. Its trailhead, just outside of Durango, is also the CT’s southern terminus. Junction Creek Trail crosses multiple footbridges over the creek along its 19-mile stretch. A video posted to Instagram highlights the Junction Creek trailhead sign that many hikers use for their CT terminus photo now standing directly at the edge of a tall wash filled with flood debris.

It has been revealed that “Junction Creek Trail #553 suffered a near-total loss in places where it parallels and crosses Junction Creek,” a USFS conditions report from November 13 reads. “Miles of trail as well as multiple bridges crossing Junction Creek were wiped out, replaced with massive piles of boulders, trees, and other flood debris.”.

It has been revealed that according to the report, both the lowest trail bridge at 2.6 miles from the trailhead and the Walls Gulch Trail Bridge at 14.6 miles were destroyed. One social media video demonstrates the first footbridge washed away completely. The USFS posted its own video of the road to Junction Creek to Facebook, showing a “20-foot waterfall” over the edge of the destroyed road.

“There is no doubt that trails across the forest have suffered severe damage,” the San Juan National Forest wrote.

According to recent reports, in an interview with The Gazette, Talley stated, “The Colorado Trail Foundation has never experienced an event that damaged this much trail. This is the largest section of trail ever damaged in our 52 years.”.

Authorities claim that recovery work will likely begin in spring and carry into summer 2027 due to weather. They discouraged hikers from even attempting to set out on the area’s trails.

“Record flooding across Southwest Colorado has left San Juan National Forest roads, trails, and other infrastructure inaccessible, severely damaged, and, in many cases, impassable,” a USDA Forest Service Facebook post reads. “Don’t become a statistic—rescue will not be readily available due to the current demand for search and rescue services.”.

The CTF remarked that it will be working over the winter with USFS, local partners, and volunteers to determine timelines and project budgets for the restoration efforts.

“It will be months before we can better understand what the next steps need to be on the sections damaged by climate events this season,” wrote Talley in his November 5 patch.

There is even less information regarding damage to the CDT, which also passes through the flood-affected areas of Southwestern Colorado.

The Continental Divide Trail Coalition (CDTC) posted on Facebook on October 23, warning hikers that flooding had made “travel to and from the CDT trailhead at Wolf Creek Pass impossible,” and that “hikers may need to make alternate prepares to avoid the area.”.

On November 2, the CDTC posted another enhancement for CDT travelers. “The extent of damage to the CDT, access roads, and CDT communities is still unknown,” it said. While the interactive map on its website reveals no current closures of the trail due to flooding, the CDTC advised hikers to use “extreme caution and check with local authorities before visiting.”.

According to recent reports, outside of Colorado, New Mexico also experienced severe flooding. However, Audra Labert with the CDTC told Backpacker, “The area of New Mexico near the southern terminus did not experience significant damage from flooding.”.

While the full extent of the damage to these trails remains to be seen, what’s certain is that the CTF, CDTC, USFS, and other state agencies have a great deal of restoration work to do next summer. Volunteers will be in high demand, and Talley, of the CTF, promised to be open about how hikers can help.

“While we do not yet know what it will take to rebuild, we do know what we will need,” Talley wrote. “We will need our supporters, we will need our dedicated volunteers, and we will need that community spirit that makes the CT so special.”.

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1580 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Trailrunnermag ↗ Open Full Page

Escape Winter With These 6 Underrated Desert Trail Runs

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1580 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission.
  • In his research for his upcoming book, “The 50 Classic Trail Runs of America” Andy Cochrane ran hundreds of trails across the U.S.
  • With all due respect to Presidential Traverse, Teton Crest, and Wonderland, the most sought-after one-day trail running route in the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

In his research for his upcoming book, “The 50 Classic Trail Runs of America” Andy Cochrane ran hundreds of trails across the U.S. These are his six favorites across the Southwest that come into season when most of the country is hibernating.

With all due respect to Presidential Traverse, Teton Crest, and Wonderland, the most sought-after one-day trail running route in the U.S. is the Grand Canyon Rim-to-Rim-to-Rim. Every spring and fall runners flock to Arizona to test their luck on this double lap of the significant ditch, despite the National Park Service strongly advising against it. (Signs around the Grand Canyon warn of heat illness, elevation, and difficult evacs.).

Some have called R2R2R an obsession—while I’m not sure I would personally go that far, I do see the argument. I’ve run the route three times and each trip I find myself more enamored than the last. On my last visit in 2023, a peak autumn weekend with nearly perfect temps and all the water facets still running (the NPS shuts some of them down seasonally), I saw hundreds of runners attempting R2R2R. That’s a tiny fraction of the four and a half million people who visit the park each year, but very busy for a trail run.

However, that was before the closures. The North Rim of the Grand Canyon was shuttered for most of the 2025 season due to the Dragon Bravo Fire, which burned 149,000 acres and 118 buildings. Then, on August 29th, 2026, a flash flood struck Phantom Ranch at the bottom of the Grand Canyon, killing three and forcing 82 others to be evacuated by helicopter. Trail damage was widespread, taking out footbridges and much of the park’s water line. The North Kaibab Trail, parts of the Bright Angel and South Kaibab trails, and sections of the River Trail remain closed with no set date for reopening.

It’s getting colder and darker across most of the country. That means one thing: It’s desert season. In lieu of a double dip into the Grand Canyon—and to open your mind to the endless possibilities elsewhere—I’ve compiled a list of my six favorite trails across the American Southwest. All of them are in my upcoming book, “The 50 Classic Trail Runs of America” (which you can pre-order now!). They cover six different states and four unique desert ecosystems, so there is plenty of variety to choose from.

Unlike the rocky singletrack of the Northeast, the forested trails of the upper Midwest, or the alpine ridges of the West, running across the Southwest desert is a singular experience. Limited shade, even less water, and direct solar radiation create obvious hydration challenges. The temperature swings dramatically from near freezing overnight to scorching heat midday. The trails themselves are a mix of surfaces, from soft sand to loose scree to firm slickrock, with many—including the ones listed below—being very remote.

According to recent reports, beyond the physical experience, running in arid environments carries a different emotion, too. I often find myself in a quiet and contemplative mental space, passing by ancient saguaros, joshua trees, and prickly pears while trying to stay alert for subtle movements of rattlesnakes, lizards, and coyotes. Running in the desert is, simultaneously, the antidote to life’s complexity and a plague of endless possibility.

There are four distinct desert ecosystems in the U.S. The northernmost is the Great Basin, which covers most of Nevada and parts of neighboring states, making it the largest desert in the country. With frigid winters, it’s filled with sagebrush instead of cacti. Just south is the Mojave, the smallest of the four, which is home to Death Valley and Joshua Tree. Further south is the Sonoran, the “green desert,” with large saguaros and rainfall in both summer and winter. Last, the Chihuahuan, covers West Texas and southern New Mexico, and is known for succulents like Agave, Yucca, and Creosote.

Sources indicate that hidden in one of North America’s most remote national parks, Big Bend, the Outer Mountain Loop is a 32-mile circuit featuring a stark ecological contrast between the Chihuahuan Desert and the high-alpine Chisos Mountains. Beginning and ending in the Chisos Basin, a sky-island that’s home to rare species like the Colima Warbler, the trail plunges down stone steps and rolls across the sun-scorched flats of the Dodson Trail before making a grueling 3,000-foot final ascent up Blue Creek Canyon. Early Spanish explorers called this isolated region El Despoblado.

Why I love it: Getting to experience both sky islands and the solitude of the Chihuahuan desert.

According to recent reports, spanning 39 miles from the edge of the Navajo Nation to the Grand Canyon’s South Rim, the Little to Major Colorado route is the less conventional way to explore one of the country’s most popular national parks. Tracing the historic Hopi salt journeys, the route plunges down Bekihatso Wash, follows the Little Colorado to its confluence with the Colorado River, passes sacred sites, scrambles obstacles like the Papago Wall, and passes by billion-year-old rock. With a 4,700-foot grind up the New Hance Trail at the end, it’s just as challenging and rewarding as rim-to-rim-to-rim.

Why I love it: It’s so close to the most famous one day trail route in the country, but still unheard of.

Crossing the national park from east to west, this 37-mile rolling route passes two distinct deserts—the higher Mojave and the lower Sonora—as you wander by long shadows of Yucca brevifolia (Joshua trees) and massive, weathered granite batholiths. Championed by the activist Minerva Hamilton Hoyt after decades of cattle grazing and mining exploitation, this sandy sanctuary strips away the crowds, offering sheer solitude as runners cross ancient mountain passes, gaze down at the dark expanse of the Salton Sea, and experience a desert communion.

Why I love it: it’s the one place in America that feels straight out of a Dr. Seuss book.

One of the most remote routes we considered for the book, this 64-mile trek traces the ridgeline of the Toiyabe Range. Like Outer Mountain, this area is a sky island, a rare ecosystem in which the valley below is a scorching hot desert, but the trail itself is a lush forest of aspen and bristlecone pines, some 3,000 years old. Despite being Nevada’s longest named trail, Toiyabe is off-trail in nature, with significant routefinding and some sections of unrunnable terrain.

Why I love it: Remote and rugged, it’s a good test of navigation and alpine movement of all sorts.

It has been revealed that perched above Albuquerque, this 26-mile trail follows a limestone ridge along the backbone of the Sandia Mountains, with 360-degree views of the Rio Grande Valley below. Sandia is Spanish for watermelon, named after the ridge’s unique sunset alpenglow that turns the cliffs deep pink, with green conifers on top representing the rind. The trail features wildflowers, ponderosas, spruce, and white fir, and can be accessed via an aerial tramway, providing easy access without sacrificing its rugged, aesthetic appeal.

Why I love it: Quick and easy access paired with absolutely beautiful sunsets.

In a recent development, winding through one of Southern Utah’s most distinctive landscapes, the 30-mile Bryce Canyon Traverse links the heavily trafficked northern amphitheater where thousands of hoodoos, rock fins, and natural arches create a natural maze with the primitive Under the Rim Trail to the south. Crossing a geological marvel shaped by erosion and freeze-thaw cycles over millions of years, the traverse is the best way to see it all. Heading southbound allows runners to catch sunrise over the spires before descending into remote backcountry, which is the direction we recommend.

Why I love it: There’s no place in the world with the same density or volume of hoodoos.

Desert running presents many challenges that the Mafate X can handle. Deserts are often oven-hot, so having a woven, high-airflow upper is ideal. They are rocky and filled with pokey things, so having a taller stack with soft PEBA foam is a bonus. They are loose, so having Vibram lugs adds a level of stability and confidence. And, with uneven ground, a wide base makes your feet feel much more planted, too.

Recent findings suggest that on long, sweaty days, sunscreen only goes so far. I take extra precaution and wear a Tahoe sun hoody, which delivers UPF 50+ protection against harsh UV rays, paired with a light polyester-spandex knit that wicks sweat off my skin and dries quickly. And, integrated thumbholes and a fitted hood keep my hands and neck completely covered without restricting movement.

For most desert runs I recommend stashing water the day before, but if you aren’t able to, having an extra large running pack is key. Kiprun’s 10L has room for a bladder in the back and two flasks up front, which is ideal for long desert stretches. The harness keeps the pack secure and large front pockets make it easy to access your phone, electrolytes, snacks, or sunscreen on the go.

My favorite drink mix, Fuel combines essential electrolytes like sodium, potassium, and magnesium to replace minerals lost in heavy sweat. It tastes good, prevents cramps, and the added zinc supports fluid retention in hot conditions. Using a low-GI carb from beet sugar, it also provides steady energy without blood sugar spikes or crashes, which is great for longer days.

  • Sitting in far West Texas along the Rio Grande, Major Bend is more than 100 miles from the nearest major city (Photo: National Guard).
  • A 19-year-old hiker is safe after falling off a cliff and staying the night on a narrow ledge in Big Bend National Park, one of the most remote national parks in the Lower 48.
  • According to a news release, on November 13, the man, whose name authorities have not released, fell ten feet when his gear gave way out in an area inaccessible to ground-based search and rescue responders.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sitting in far West Texas along the Rio Grande, Major Bend is more than 100 miles from the nearest major city (Photo: National Guard).

A 19-year-old hiker is safe after falling off a cliff and staying the night on a narrow ledge in Big Bend National Park, one of the most remote national parks in the Lower 48.

According to a news release, on November 13, the man, whose name authorities have not released, fell ten feet when his gear gave way out in an area inaccessible to ground-based search and rescue responders. Rescuers reached the area just after 9 P.M. and called the Georgia Army National Guard medical evacuation crew assigned to the Joint Task Force-Southern Border. The organization works with U.S. Customs and Border Protection to monitor the shared border between Texas and Mexico, an area central to a heated national debate over the Trump Administration’s border wall construction.

The helicopter crew had taken off, but with limited lighting and winds approaching 35 miles per hour, and a string of storms moving into the area, the Black Hawk medevac crew made the difficult decision to scrub the mission.

According to recent reports, “The crew agreed it was not safe and we had to make the unfortunate decision to go back and try again in the daylight,” Chief Warrant Officer 2 Gregory Hiett, the aircraft commander, said in a statement. “It was an extremely difficult thing to do, knowing the patient was going to be stuck out there for the rest of the night.”.

Throughout the night, park responders remained on-scene and on the ground.

Just after 9 A.M. on November 14, a second helicopter mission rolled out with a hoist rescue team. Flight medic and technician Holly Johnson descended 150 feet on a cable, determined the hiker was uninjured, and secured him in a rescue vest to lift him into the aircraft. The mission was finished by 10:45 A.M., and the hiker was transferred to Major Bend Regional Medical Center.

“During a complex hoist operation in rugged, inaccessible terrain, our medevac crew successfully reached and evacuated an injured hiker when no ground rescue option existed, delivering the patient safely to higher medical care,” Lt. Col. Teresa Parrotta, commander of the 29th Combat Aviation Brigade, Maryland Army National Guard, remarked in a statement.

Sources indicate that sitting in far West Texas along the Rio Grande, Big Bend is more than 100 miles from the nearest major city. It’s rugged, isolated, and enormous, spanning 800,000 acres with sheer 1,500-foot limestone cliffs. The National Park Service warns visitors to expect unreliable cell service, sparse infrastructure, and primitive roads—conditions compounded by the intense Chihuahuan Desert sandwiched between the Chisos Mountains. Reaching a hiking trailhead is challenging because roads frequently wash out from flash flooding, and many backcountry trails require high-clearance, four-wheel-drive vehicles.

NOAA Just Tweaked Its Winter Forecast. Here’s What’s Changed for Skiers.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) has some encouraging news for skiers hoping for a major rebound after last winter’s dismal snow season, particularly in California and the Southwest.
  • Sources indicate that the agency’s Climate Prediction Center released its latest winter outlook on Thursday, Nov.
  • Sources indicate that the fresh forecast tweaks a few things from its previous iterations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Courtesy of Taos Ski Valley).

The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) has some encouraging news for skiers hoping for a major rebound after last winter’s dismal snow season, particularly in California and the Southwest.

Sources indicate that the agency’s Climate Prediction Center released its latest winter outlook on Thursday, Nov. 19, updating its forecast for the months ahead. The biggest development? The odds of above-average precipitation have increased across California and the Desert Southwest, offering a more promising outlook for a couple of the ski regions that have struggled with snow in recent years.

Sources indicate that the fresh forecast tweaks a few things from its previous iterations. Here’s a cheat sheet, but be sure to read on for more specifics and a regional breakdown:.

Recent findings suggest that finally, NOAA claims that the fresh precipitation forecasts are more reliable than their temperature forecasts this winter, which they attribute to the strong El Niño and an active southern storm track. In other words, there will be moisture, but there’s no guarantee it’ll come down as snow.

Here’s what the updated outlook says:.

The latest outlook favors above-average precipitation across the southern United States, stretching from southwestern Oregon and California through the Desert Southwest and into the southern Plains and Southeast.

Recent findings suggest that for ski country, California and the Southwest stand out. NOAA increased the probabilities of above-average precipitation in both regions compared with its previous outlook. Southern California and southwestern Arizona now have greater than a 60 percent chance of finishing the December-through-February period wetter than average.

That could be welcome news for resorts in the Sierra Nevada, including Mammoth and the Lake Tahoe region, as well as Arizona Snowbowl and Upcoming Mexico’s Taos Ski Valley and Ski Santa Fe. The forecast also offers some encouragement for southern Colorado, including Purgatory, Wolf Creek, and Telluride, although it’s far less clear for the Front Range and Northern Rockies.

Recent findings suggest that it’s worth noting here that NOAA is forecasting total precipitation, not snowfall, per se. Whether that moisture falls as snow or rain will depend on temperatures, snow levels, and where individual storms track. Still, a wetter-than-average winter would be a step in the right direction.

NOAA continues to favor below-average precipitation across parts of the northern Rockies. The region also faces an increased likelihood of higher than average temperatures, a combo that’s not music to the ears of resorts in Montana, Idaho, and Wyoming. The Pacific Northwest also faces odds of warmer-than-average temperatures, particularly across Washington and Oregon.

In a recent development, elsewhere, the outlook favors wetter-than-average conditions across much of the East Coast and Southeast. However, warmer temperatures could complicate snowfall prospects, particularly at lower-elevation ski areas.

Industry observers note that this is the latest chapter in a winter forecast that skiers have been watching closely for months. Earlier this summer, NOAA’s increasingly confident projections of a potentially historic El Niño raised hopes for a snowy rebound across parts of the West following last season’s exceptionally poor conditions.

In July, SKI spoke with meteorologists and ski-travel experts about what the developing climate pattern could mean for the upcoming season. The early consensus pointed toward the Southwest, particularly southern Colorado, Newly introduced Mexico, Arizona, and California, as regions with favorable odds for an active storm track. Much of that remains the same.

But there were plenty of question marks, and there still are, namely what will happen in central Colorado and Utah. NOAA’s earlier outlook showed average precipitation for those destinations, and the latest forecast is slightly more encouraging. We still recommend choosing higher elevation ski areas to pad your odds for snow rather than rain.

It has been revealed that NOAA’s next seasonal outlook is scheduled for December 17. Until then, skiers will have to keep watching the shorter-range forecasts and hope the promising signals translate into the kind of winter the West desperately needs.
