  • Fred Rogers was so good at so many things — rocking a cardigan, controlling puppets, speaking very straightforwardly to children— that it often obscures another skill: he was a damn fine musician, writing a performing hundreds of songs during the show’s masterful run.
  • Recent findings suggest that the same is true for Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood, to an extent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The anthems of Mister Rogers'might not be ones that make you bust out your lighter, but then again, maybe you should?

Fred Rogers was so good at so many things — rocking a cardigan, controlling puppets, speaking very straightforwardly to children— that it often obscures another skill: he was a damn fine musician, writing a performing hundreds of songs during the show’s masterful run. Figuring out the best Mister Rogers’ songs is mostly all about thinking about why the series was so successful to begin with. Part of the reason why a piece of kids’ entertainment stands the test of time is nearly always connected to music. The reason we still love Sleeping Beauty is because of the brilliant way Disney adapted the classic ballet by Tchaikovsky and, essentially, turned that music into a bunch of pop songs. Nobody thinks about it, but the great visuals in kids’ entertainment are almost always not the reason something is amazing.

Recent findings suggest that the same is true for Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood, to an extent. Yes, we love Fred Rogers’ style, but arguably, the words he spoke and the songs are the real reason the show is so enduring. Contemporarily, the descendant of Mister Rogers; Daniel Tiger’s Neighborhood, also finds its way into the hearts and minds of children through the helpful songs. And though I think some of the Daniel Tiger songs are great, it’s hard to top the originals from Fred himself.

Here are nine songs from Fred Rogers, ranked in order of how memorable and how good they will make you feel.

Industry observers note that I call this one the Mister Rogers version of the ’80s anthem “Relax.” Same energy. Same vibe. But, I think Fred Rogers does this concept better than Frankie Goes to Hollywood, don’t you?

Recent findings suggest that chances are if you’ve heard this song, you remember it from the very famous speech Mister Rogers gave when he addressed the U.S. Senate. Because this is one of his famous songs that deals with complicated feelings, it’s obviously one of his best. It’s a bit of a talking-through-it song, which is like the Rogers version of Bob Dylan impression, except every word is impeccably enunciated.

Industry observers note that there’s a Daniel Tiger song called “We Are Friends.” My daughter likes it a lot. But, the thing is, this song is way better.

Industry observers note that I have a very strong memory of this song, and I imagine kids who grew up in the ’80s are with me. There’s something about the sentiment of it, combined with the sweetness that really, really stick in your mind. The truth will make you free! He’s right, obviously, but there’s something more magical about it than just that. He’s right, and if you sing along, you can be forgiven for whatever stupid little kid stuff you did. Magic.

If Mister Rogers was Taylor Swift this would be his biggest hit single. This song is great for kids who have just learned the word “fancy,” but also for adults who need to think about their inner-fanciness. A song that is equally good for right before bedtime with your kids, or a boozy brunch with your buddies.

Sources indicate that once we start getting into the top of this list, the songs are basically great because they are absurdly sweet. Still, the message of this one has some intelligence behind it. And, I suspect Paul McCartney wished he’d written it.

Feeling safe is probably the most important thing for a child. The reason why Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood worked so well is that the idea of security and comfort was built into everything about the series. And this song is the musical version of that philosophy.

Industry observers note that you know this one by heart. You’re humming it right now. Not just one of the best Mister Rogers songs of all time, but probably one of the best children’s songs, period. Plus, the bass player is taking it for a walk.

The theme song of a TV show is usually memorable in connection with that show and, therefore, hard to really care about in another context. Like, the theme for Knight Rider; you can’t hear it without thinking about David Hasselhoff, several buttons unbuttoned on a shirt, and a talking car. “Won’t You Be My Neighbor” is like that for Fred Rogers. If you hear you, can picture him taking off his shoes, meticulously. And the reverse works, too. If you take your shoes off slowly and calmly, you’ll be humming this tune.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Is there anything more whimsical, more magical than the idea of being able to befriend a crow?

With the ability to recognize individual people, remember faces and learn from experience, these glossy-feathered birds are among the cleverest birds we're likely to encounter in our gardens. They're also steeped in symbolism, appearing in various traditions as spiritual messengers or guides associated with wisdom, transformation and the mysteries of life.

For those who enjoy looking for a little meaning in the natural world, then, spotting one could feel like more than just another garden bird sighting. Especially if you're the sort of person who obsesses over your birth month bird, or spends ages wondering what the first bird you see each morning claims about your day ahead.

Sources indicate that look, we all love finding little stories and connections in nature. Indeed, some of us even believe that the bird we see most in our garden indicates everything about our gardening style – and a regular crow visitor might suggest there's something rather welcoming about your outdoor space. So, yes, it makes sense many of us are secretly wondering how to befriend a crow.

If you've been on social media lately, you may have stumbled across the (admittedly niche) trend of CrowTok, which sees people share videos of their feathered visitors, the food they leave out and, occasionally, the curious little objects their avian friends appear to bring in return. And while we might like to imagine these offerings are thank-you gifts, there's some fascinating science behind the behaviour.

Yes, the National Audubon Society has explored how crows sometimes leave objects for people who feed them, with corvid biologist John Marzluff explaining that a clever bird could learn that leaving an object results in a tasty reward.

Industry observers note that it's a lovely reminder that our relationship with nature can be full of surprises. Crows are social and remarkably observant birds, and while they're wild animals rather than pets, they can learn to recognise familiar faces and become more comfortable around people who treat them consistently and respectfully.

In a recent development, so, if you'd love to befriend a crow and see a few more of these clever characters dropping by your backyard, there are some simple ways to make your outdoor space more appealing. From offering their favorite snacks to creating a safe spot where they can stop for a drink, here's how to attract crows to your yard – and perhaps even earn their trust in the process.

If there's one way to catch a crow's attention, it's with a tasty snack. Peanuts are a popular choice, and unsalted peanuts are a good option to offer. You could also try a little variety with other suitable foods, such as cooked eggs (plain, obviously, so hold the seasoning!) or mealworms.

It's not just what you offer that matters, however; it's how regularly you do it. Environment for the Americas recommends putting food and water out at the same time and in the same place each day, as crows are intelligent enough to recognise routines, and may soon learn when to expect a visit.

According to recent reports, start by putting out a small amount, then, and clear away anything uneaten to avoid attracting unwanted visitors. With time, your regular visitors may begin to recognize you as the person responsible for their daily delivery.

Crows are naturally cautious birds, so where you put their food can make a substantial difference if you're trying to make friends with one. Rather than hiding snacks away in a traditional hanging bird feeder, then, try placing a small amount on a low feeding platform or another suitable open surface (like this nifty Deck Bird Feeder from Amazon).

A spot near a fence, shed roof or sturdy tree branch can give them somewhere to perch while they tuck in. And, ideally, you should choose somewhere with clear sightlines, as this allows crows to keep an eye on their surroundings and spot potential danger.

Try to give them plenty of space, too. If you're watching from indoors, they'll have the opportunity to get comfortable with your presence without feeling as though they're being observed too closely.

Sources indicate that food might get their attention, but a reliable source of fresh water can give crows another reason to visit. Try placing a shallow bird bath or sturdy water bowl somewhere accessible, with a gently sloping edge that makes it easy for birds to drink and bathe.

Keep the water fresh, changing it regularly and cleaning the dish to prevent a build-up of dirt and bacteria. Position it somewhere relatively open so visiting crows can watch for potential predators while they stop for a drink... and then get ready for the most tedious part of our How To Befriend A Crow 101 Guide: be patient.

Industry observers note that oh yes, rather than rushing outside to get closer, try sitting quietly at a distance while the birds eat and drink. Some crow enthusiasts on Reddit also suggest making a gentle whistling sound as you put food out, as this helps the birds associate that sound with a reliable food source, but that one is well and truly up to you!

Recent findings suggest that it takes time to befriend a crow. Give it a little while, though, and you may find that your visitors become less wary when you're around. Just let them set the pace – earning the trust of a wild crow is a relationship worth taking slowly.

Sure, you might not end up with a crow delivering shiny little presents to your doorstep, but creating a garden where these intelligent birds feel safe enough to visit? Well, that's a rather lovely reward in itself, I say!

She previously served as digital editor at Stylist magazine, and has written extensively for Ideal Home, Woman & Home, Homes & Gardens, and a handful of other titles. As such, her garden – designed around the stunning magnolia tree at its centre – is filled to the brim with pollinator-friendly blooms, homemade bird feeders, and old logs for insects to nest in.

They help you do everything from block problematic sites to set weekly screen-time limits.

Sources indicate that smartphones are small miracles. If your kid has a smartphone, they have access to the world’s accumulated knowledge and whatever TikTok is. Unfortunately, owning a smartphone also means access to porn, violent imagery, and other disturbing content that they’re just not mature enough to see. The other massive risk: constantly disappearing into the world of the phone, much of which is designed to be addictive, and not participating enough in real life.

Sources indicate that thankfully, with the rise of these smartphones has come a number of parental-control devices and apps that help you do everything from block problematic sites to set weekly screen-time limits. These six apps, in particular, are excellent tools for monitoring your kids’ usage and setting parameters on what they’re able to see. They’re a must for parents worried that a smartphone might screw their kid up.

A continual parent favorite, the OurPact Parental Control and Kid Tracker is our pick for best-in-show if you want a little bit of everything. Control screen-time limits, block apps, locate, track, and shut down texts: This one does it all, and it does it all well. There’s even another app, OurPact Jr., that gives kids the information they need regarding their screen-time allowance and schedules. (Free, $2, and $7 monthly plans).

Recent findings suggest that question: What to do for the kid who chews through every game put in front of him or her? Answer: Azoomee. This curated app includes over 1,000 games, puzzles, and activities, all of which have some kind of educational component designed for kids 5 and older. Sometimes, the easiest way to keep an eye on the kid is to trust the digital environment you put them into. (Free version includes access to a small selection of content; premium is $6.50 monthly, $33 for six months, or $59 for the year).

Available on: Apple App Store and Google Play.

Sources indicate that covenant Eyes is an effective porn blocker that will make sure your kids don’t stumble across inernet smut. Once installed it bleaches content from search engines (including when said search engines are accessed through other sites) and YouTube. Should an attempt to gain access be made, a report is sent to you. (Free).

Available on: Apple App Store and Google Play.

Industry observers note that as fathers, we want to trust our kids with their own devices, and that’s why Google Family Link is so important. For children under 13, the app manages the apps on their devices, controls screen time, and establishes a bedtime, all while still allowing for installed apps to update. Keep in mind that, while you can monitor your kid’s phone if it’s an iOS device, you can only lock it down it if they have an Android phone. (Free).

Available on: Apple App Store and Google Play.

True, Kaspersky Safe Kids Family GPS offers some of the features you’d expect from a parental control app, such as customizable website blocking, safe search, remote permission granting, app and device usage, and more. But it’s the premium service that distinguishes it from its peers. Once they pay, parents can go beyond just checking their kid’s current location. Should your child leave his or her designated “safe space” you’ll receive an alert. You’ll also receive alerts for suspicious activity and social media monitoring of new friends. Android customers can also monitor their texts and calls. (Free; Premium for $12/year).

Available on: Apple App Store and Google Play.

In a recent development, mobicip covers computers, and Mobicip Parental Controls covers smartphones. In short, if your child is using anything short of a library book for research, this app is tracking, filtering, and protecting them. Customize by age, establish a time limit, filter YouTube, and, at the end of the day, receive a report on activities. And since it’s based in the cloud, kids can’t simply switch from wifi to 4LTE to escape its safety net. ($40/year to protect up to five devices).

Available on: Apple App Store, Google Play, Google Chrome, Windows, macOS.

Industry observers note that katie Leigh Matthews is a contributing writer for Moms.com. As the mom of a sweet and sensitive 9-year-old boy and a wild and free 5-year-old girl, she brings her ever-evolving experience of parenting to everything she writes.

It has been revealed that she’s been writing forever, and professionally for three years. Towards that end, she writes often on introversion and the trait of high sensitivity to highlight their strengths and promote more self-compassion among all who share them. She regularly collaborates with experts in these fields to create content that informs, encourages, and empowers.

She loves that through Moms.com, she can put her chronic overthinking of every parenting decision to good use by saving readers time and hopefully a headache or two.

Recent findings suggest that katie lives in Birmingham, Alabama, with her husband and two kids. On any given day she’s probably either rewatching her favorite shows for the 100th time or dipping her toes in any creek she can find.

Industry observers note that you’ve booked your tickets. You’ve planned your itinerary. You’ve figured out the My Disney Experience App (you think.) You’re as ready as you can be for your family’s first trip to Disney World. Then it dawns on you: What do you need to pack? Shopping for essentials for your first family trip to Disney World is an art – it’s about knowing your family and what you all need to thrive on one of the most exciting, most magical, and yes, sometimes stressful family vacations.

It has been revealed that A little online searching will promptly convince you you'll need to buy extra luggage just to pack park essentials, but don’t stress. As an easily-overwhelmed mom who recently braved Disney World for the first time, I've got some hard-won advice to help guide your vacation prep and inform your packing list. Plus, I've scoured the internet for top picks of the most-used sanity-saving products to make the happiest place on earth live up to its name for you and your family.

For many parents, taking the kids to Disney World at least once during their childhood is a bucket list goal. When that dream is finally realized, there is a mix of idyllic anticipation and anxious uncertainty. It’s not surprising that many parents find planning for a trip to Disney World to be a stressful experience.

Recent findings suggest that when it comes to Disney World, there are two types of parents: those who have fond memories of their own childhood Disney vacation, and those who hope to give their own kids the trip they didn’t get to experience growing up. Whichever type you are, the goal is the same: To give your kids a core-memory-making family vacation they’ll cherish forever. Of course, a love of Disney also evokes childhood nostalgia that is so fun to share with your own children. The legacy of classic and modern Disney characters, movies, and parks is a special thing to pass on to the next generation and something that carries a lot of weight for many.

In a recent development, along with all the hopes and expectations wrapped up in a family trip to Disney World, the cost of the vacation only adds to the pressure to make it the best trip ever. For budget travelers, the average weeklong Disney World vacation for a family of four can cost $6,000 or more, according to NerdWallet, so ensuring you get your money’s worth is a huge factor. Not only that, but with so much to see, do, and experience in the parks, a vacation to Disney World is a complex trip to plan. Some families even turn to Disney vacation planners and travel agents to help with the sheer volume of logistical planning involved.

It has been revealed that as tempting as it may be, you don’t need to add-to-cart every single item you see on ‘Must Have Disney Essentials’ lists. Before you start shopping, it pays to think through what will help your family enjoy your trip the most. The best travel products for families will vary, so evaluate these factors before you start shopping:.

Industry observers note that of course, start with the makeup of your family. How old will your kids be on the trip, and what needs and preferences correspond with their ages? Strollers are a big decision for many, and there are lots of pros and cons to consider: Will it help or hurt to have a stroller for airports? Is it worth it to lug a stroller to the parks? Would renting Disney World strollers be a better option? The answer will be different for every family, so don’t listen to advice that insists on a right answer. Our youngest was six on our trip and I seriously considered taking or renting a stroller. She ended up walking the parks like a champ and I was glad we didn’t have to deal with a stroller! Had she been a year younger, though, I am sure a stroller would have been our saving grace.

According to recent reports, what are your kids most looking forward to in the parks? How will they handle long lines? Will you need to anticipate an afternoon nap each day? Should you stock up on a few fun toys ahead of time so your kiddos aren’t pining for the theme park loot, or do you just need to upgrade your child’s luggage? A Disney World vacation will look very different depending on the ages of your kids, so narrow your list of essentials based on them.

Recent findings suggest that A surefire way to preemptively ruin your first trip to Disney World is to forget your own needs in the process. For parents, Disney World is fun, sure, but there’s also a lot of planning, incessant crowds, unrelenting heat, not to mention the never-ending soundboard of the kids' needs and wants. Take a moment and think about what essentials you need to make the most of the trip, and perhaps even a few indulgent spa day gifts to help melt stress away at the end of a non-stop Disney World day.

A travel-size umbrella that offers heavy-duty weather protection.

Recent findings suggest that weather is a big factor in whether Disney World lives up to being “the happiest place on earth.” You likely know to expect warmer temperatures year-round, and extreme heat in the summer. But surprise rain showers are also a common occurrence in Orlando. Luckily, the Repel Compact Umbrella can help on both fronts. Not only will you be happy you have it if you get caught in a shower, but it will also filter UV rays when the sun is beating down. In fact, Repel even offers a UPF 50+ UV protection version of the umbrella to block out 99% of UV rays.

The umbrella's double-vented canopy is designed to withstand winds up to 85 MPH, so you won’t have to worry about it inverting. It is a heavy-duty umbrella packed into a compact travel size, opens and collapses with a push of a button, and is definitely worth tossing in your park bag. Reviewers say it performs as advertised – one even remarked the umbrella “loves wind” – with just a few saying the only concern they’ve had is closing it. (And yes, Disney World does allow umbrellas!).

This microfiber towel will save the day in all sorts of ways when you’re out and about, and packs into its own travel bag.

Sources indicate that when you’re at the parks from sun up to sun down, unexpected needs are bound to arise, and the Rainleaf Microfiber Towel will be a lifesaver for many of them. Kid drop Dole Whip down their shirt? Want to dry off a wet seat? Need to add more sun shade to the stroller? Chances are you’ll be reaching for this towel all day long. Not only is it compact and made for travel, but it also absorbs five times its own weight and dries incredibly fast. If it’s super hot, drench the towel in cold water to help you cool off, then drape it over your backpack or stroller as you walk around to let it air dry.

Running from $9 to $20 a piece, depending on the size, it’s worth giving each family member their own, or grabbing a few to designate for certain purposes – one for clean up, one for shade and sweat, and one as a picnic blanket for parades or just a quick rest.

This compact travel charger keeps your devices topped up all day long.

Between taking a million pictures and using the Disney app to do everything from making meal orders and reservations to finding the next ride (or nearest restroom!), you’ll be using your phone a lot in the parks. The Anker Portable Charger ensures your devices stay charged up all day long. It has a universal USB-C cable and delivers 10,000mAh (milliamp hours), delivering the equivalent of two full smartphone charges. At 30W charging speed, you can expect it to fully charge a phone in about an hour – which is how long you’ll be lining for some rides anyway.

In a recent development, the charger is just a tad bigger than a credit card, and weighs about as much as a phone. It can charge three devices at once (you just need extra charging cables) and the cable connector stores in the battery pack for safekeeping between uses. Coming in under $30, it’s well worth the peace of mind so you don’t miss a single picture-perfect moment, even as the last firework illuminates the night sky.

One tip I got from a Disney World cast member is to take screenshots of the QR codes, order confirmations, lightning lane arrival windows, and anything else you may need for reference from the My Disney Experience App so you aren’t constantly having to access the app, which can drain your phone battery.

Take a rest whenever you need to with this super practical compact folding stool.

In a recent development, the Boreeman Folding Stool is as close as it gets to realizing the idea of pants that turn into a chair, but arguably way more practical. If your back just isn’t what it used to be, or you’ve got a kiddo who you know will complain about standing in line, this folding stool will single-handedly save your Disney World trip. The collapsible seat locks into place at various heights up to 17.72 inches. It packs down into a disc that is 9.84 inches by 2.36 inches with a carrying strap for added convenience. Use it in ride lines, waiting for parades or reveals, or just whenever you need to take a load off. It also comes in handy to help little ones with bathroom needs.

Recent findings suggest that the stool is highly rated with 4.4 stars from over 8,000 reviewers, but some say it’s not super comfortable, while others warn theirs broke while sitting on it. Still, other reviewers say they still use theirs often over a year later. It comes in tons of fun colors and can slide into bags, backpacks, or stroller compartments. It’s also light enough at 2.5 pounds for many kids to carry it through a ride line themselves.

Make any moment magical with these Disney-themed bubble wands.

The struggle to not buy every cute thing you see in Disney World is real, and the Little Kids Disney Light and Sound Musical Bubble Wand is here to help. Light-up bubble wands are all the rage in the parks, and they come with a hefty price tag. If you’re looking to save money where you can on your trip, surprise your little one with a pre-bought bubble wand for a fraction of the cost of the park varieties, which cost upwards of $35.

Industry observers note that these wands are themed with all their favorite characters, including Mickey Mouse, Tiana, Elsa, Moana, and more. They light up, play music, and come with extra bubbles so your kiddo can join in the bubble wand fun all day long. Some reviewers were not satisfied with the durability and quality of the wand, while others say it was perfect for their Disney Parks trip.

Outsmart unpredictable weather with this family pack of reusable ponchos.

My family didn’t end up needing the Lingito Rain Ponchos Family Pack for rain, but we were so glad we used them on Tiana’s Bayou Adventure! We got in one of the first virtual queue time slots of the morning, and without the ponchos, we would have been utterly soaked for the rest of the day. This family pack gets the job done at keeping your family (and your backpacks) dry, whether the water is weather or ride-related. The adult ponchos have drawstrings, and while I understand they might pose a hazard for kids, I wish the kid ponchos could tighten for a better fit. My kids held theirs closed just under their chins when we dropped down the log flume.

They come compactly packed in small disposable bags, and you’ll be hard-pressed to fold them back in after you open them. The Amazon listing describes these ponchos as both reusable and disposable, which is accurate. While they can be dried out and used again on a trip, they might be too much trouble to save for your next adventure (however, one reviewer reports their family has used their set again and again). Still, at $10 for a pack of four (two adult and two kid-sized ponchos), they are well worth throwing in your bag every day in case you get caught in one of those notorious surprise Orlando rain showers – or just so you stay dry on wet rides.

This wearable fan rests around your neck for hands-free cooling wherever you go.

If you're worried about the relentless Orlando heat more than any other part of your Disney trip, do yourself a favor and pack the FrSara Portable Neck Fan. It’s encased blade vents blow air all the way around the back of the neck and out the ends to keep you noticeably cooler without having to worry about hazards like tangling hair. With a noise level of 25 dB – the equivalent of the ambient noise of a ‘silent’ PC – you can even keep it running indoors through those winding ride lines without being a nuisance to yourself or others …though it’s worth noting that some reviewers find it too loud.

Recent findings suggest that the fan's working time ranges from four to 16 hours, and its USB-C charging port means you can recharge on the go with a portable device charger. With three speeds and 360-degree surround airflow, it might not quite make you forget you’re in Orlando, but it can certainly take the edge off the heat.

This lightweight travel stroller folds down easily and has four recline positions with tons of storage.

To pack a stroller or not to pack a stroller, that is the question for families making the pilgrimage to Disney World. If you decide to bring your own, the Summer Infant 3Dlite Stroller is our pick for Disney World for a few reasons. First, the stroller complies with Disney World’s list of prohibited items regarding stroller size, and reviewers do confirm that they used this stroller in Disney World. Second, the price is right at under $100, though it’s worth noting that single-stroller rentals at Disney World go for $15 per day, and $13 per day for multi-day rentals.

According to recent reports, the stroller is lightweight, has four recline positions for napping on the go, a pop out weather canopy, and tons of extra storage, including a cup holder, close-top bag, and large storage compartment underneath the seat. Reiewers agree that this is a great, budget-friendly stroller for travel, and is highly rated at 4.6 stars with over 7,000 reviews. Plus, it has a weight capacity of 50 pounds, which is on the upper end for most travel strollers. So if you have an older kid who might not be able to last the entire day on foot, this stroller can be a lifesaver.

Take it from me, even anxious, stressed-out parents can make the most of their family’s first trip to Disney World. Resolve to manage your stress level by taking good care of yourself, setting yourself up for success by planning based on what will make it magical for your family, and packing essentials that will help everyone enjoy the trip.

The key is managing expectations, especially your own. Knowing that a vacation with kids is still parenting, just in a different location – and understanding that parenting in Disney World isn’t always a walk in the park – can help you make this trip every bit as magical for your kiddos as you hoped, though it likely won’t feel like it to you. So make sure you stop and take in their sweet faces when they meet their favorite characters, when they go on the ride they were so excited for, and as they watch as fireworks illuminate the night. You’ll experience the magic, guaranteed!

How to Talk to Kids, According to Mister Rogers

📅 31 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (952 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • What would Mister Rogers say to kids in these strange, difficult, and uncertain times?
  • It has been revealed that how can we talk to our kids when we’re feeling some child-like fear and frustration ourselves?
  • Mister Rogers knew how to talk to kids, in part because the brilliant child psychologist Dr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a good time to get fluent in Freddish.

What would Mister Rogers say to kids in these strange, difficult, and uncertain times? It can be hard to grasp how a child’s mind works: I’m often thrown by the way my 3-year-old makes logical leaps that are alternatingly brilliant and disjointed, with wild emotions, good and bad, clouding her perception of the world. It can be hard to know what to do with all those knotted feelings and ideas, especially in times of universal stress, with all normalcy temporarily knocked down by the coronavirus pandemic.

It has been revealed that how can we talk to our kids when we’re feeling some child-like fear and frustration ourselves? How do we make kids feel safe and secure, while giving them space to share their feelings? How do you speak to a child in their language? And, perhaps more vital, how do you understand them when they speak back?

Mister Rogers knew how to talk to kids, in part because the brilliant child psychologist Dr. Margaret McFarland was his mentor. Operating in the shadow of Benjamin Spock during his Pittsburgh tenure and afterwards (and whose work would not age nearly as well), McFarland focused on meaning. She understood that, to a child, a bee is not just a bee. It’s an existential threat. She offered Fred Rogers these insights and a view into the complex interplay of language and feelings, as they’re experienced by children (which she drew partly from her study of mothers’ interactions with their babies). McFarland helped rework most of the scripts for Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood and the results speaks for itself: The show has quietly captivated children for decades.

Recent findings suggest that naturally, those around Fred Rogers credited him with inventing the language he spoke. He didn’t. Neither did McFarland. They learned it, and Rogers became the most prominent American to speak it both publicly and fluently. This language came to be known among the crew at KQED, where Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood was filmed, as Freddish. It is, in short, the language of children.

Industry observers note that like any language, Freddish is not simply a collection of words. Grammar comes with it. Manners, too. It’s easy to think that Mister Rogers cast a spell by speaking simply — and that certainly helped — but it was his clarity and inclusiveness that helped him stand apart. The phrasing was always precise, not clouded by inadvertent negativity or stress. The slow pace, defined by all those pauses, allowed room for kids who were watching to think, to look, and to respond.

According to recent reports, the Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood staff were so impressed by Rogers’s ability to speak to children that they wrote a translation manual. Written in jest, but extraordinarily accurate, “Let’s Talk About Freddish,” offers nine commandments of communication that collectively serve as a guide to speaking to young children in a way that facilitates understanding and comfort.

The precepts, which appear in Maxwell King’s The Good Neighbor: The Life and Work of Fred Rogers, are as follows….

According to recent reports, the manual is an excellent tool to use when interacting with your child. I might not be able to go through the entire nine-step process or have the time — or, let’s face it, the emotional energy — to speak as thoughtfully as Rogers did. But even keeping in mind one guideline, which is what I’m starting with, makes a difference.

Sources indicate that with most languages, translation is a matter of matching similar words with similar functions. Translating to Freddish, however, is about identifying emotions and relationships as well as words. The goal is to communicate a clear sense of purpose and to provide support while also introducing an idea. The evolution of an adult thought into a Freddish expression would look, in our house, something like this….

I have a lot to learn when it comes to talking to my daughter: I sound nothing like Number 9. But I have even more to learn about listening — something that Mister Rogers also knew how to do. Watch any episode and you’ll see and hear Rogers leaving quiet space around his words so kids could respond or make observations; making the most of simple, open-ended comments like “Oh,” which allows kids to draw their own conclusions; asking lots and lots of questions, which gives kids a chance to participate in the conversation and feel — incredibly, for a TV show — that the attention is on them.

The pacing of Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood can make the show difficult to watch. It’s slow. But that slowness is a product of discipline, and that discipline pays dividends. Adopting that slowness and communicating with purpose is incredibly difficult, but when I manage the trick, I can see my daughter respond. She stops using her favorite daycare expression — “You stepped on my words” — and starts communicating more directly as she senses that I’m listening and not jumping in.

It has been revealed that I’ve stopped asking my daughter, “What is it?” when she reveals me a drawing. I ask her to tell me about it — and she does. I’m starting to explain more clearly what I ask of her and the reason why. I’m learning to wait while she finds the exact words to explain that her play food is “hair ketchup” that she’s pouring on her head. It can be confusing at times, slow at others, but I understand that it’s my job to sort through what comes out, and Freddish helps. Asking questions helps. Being quiet helps.

#91006. Latest Update: The 5 Words Mister Rogers Used Most And How They Help Kids Learn

📅 31 Jul 2025 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1342 w)
📖 Baca

Latest Update: The 5 Words Mister Rogers Used Most And How They Help Kids Learn

📅 31 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1342 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, want to build a bridge to better communication with children.
  • The way Fred Rogers communicated has been the subject of much examination.
  • According to recent reports, we know that Fred Rogers created a space of encouragement and kindness, but by examining which words he leaned on, we can learn to construct meaning and child-friendly lessons out of Mister Rogers’ rhetorical building blocks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, want to build a bridge to better communication with children. Use the building blocks that Fred Rogers Used.

The way Fred Rogers communicated has been the subject of much examination. He was deliberate without being rigid. He was quiet without being passive. He was empathetic without being paralyzed. How did he achieve this? He worked hard at his scripts. In his archive in Pennsylvania, stacks of scribble-covered papers pay tribute to Rogers as an exacting self-editor. The printed scripts contain large words that were then carefully crossed out and replaced with more comprehensible language. After all, Mister Rogers, the titular character and de facto mayor of Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood, spoke mostly to coma and to the millions of children watching in their homes. He understood that they hung on his every word. But what were those words, exactly?

According to recent reports, we know that Fred Rogers created a space of encouragement and kindness, but by examining which words he leaned on, we can learn to construct meaning and child-friendly lessons out of Mister Rogers’ rhetorical building blocks. To that end, Fatherly analyzed the closed-captioning text for 30 representative episodes of Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood pulled from the 31-season run. After throwing out common words (conjunctions, articles, pronouns), we looked at the frequency of word use. The results show that Mister Rogers was not merely a calm and affirming character. He insisted on exploration and action. He demanded curiosity. And he responded to it as well.

In a recent development, A breakdown of Mister Rogers’ most frequently used words provides a window into a spectacularly effective communication strategy. And his top five words by usage are a great place to start.

It makes sense that a cornerstone of educational children’s programming like Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood would make knowing central. To know is to be educated and to understand. But for Fred Rogers, the verb was dynamic and transactional. The knowing went both ways. Yes, he wanted his young audience to know the world through the lens of their neighborhood, but he also wanted to know his young audience.

In Mister Rogers’ world, “know” is frequently part of a question. Rogers doesn’t assume a child’s knowledge or demand that they know much of anything. But he uses knowing to pique curiosity: “Did you know…?” or “Do you know…?” has the power to draw children into discovery. The word places a primacy on the act of seeking an answer, and assures children that the world can be known. In that way, Rogers could inspire kids to be curious themselves, while also reassuring them that there was an answer to be found. Rogers is often remembered for the emotional resonance of his work, but he was not just interested in feelings. He loved to empower children with facts. The feeling of security he inspired emerged from the sense that Mister Rogers was never evasive. He wanted his audience to know what he knew.

Industry observers note that many viewers of Mister Rogers Neighborhood will remember the factory visits. Viewer were often taken to various spots near the WQED studios in Pittsburgh to learn how things were made. We were given a glimpse into the process of making so we could see that the things in our homes didn’t simply appear there fully formed. There were steps in making paper, or violins or rubber balls.

Sources indicate that rogers loved the idea of manufacturing. In the Neighborhood of Make-Believe the puppet Cornflake S. Pecially calls himself a man that manufactures. He makes chairs. And there are often plots that revolve around Cornflakes’ chair-making factory. Cornflake was one of the first puppets Fred Rogers ever made.

Sources indicate that but aside from showing his young viewers how things were made, Mister Rogers often invited children into his kitchen, to sit with him a the table and craft. The projects would usually involve materials found around the home — a protean form of upcycling before the term was even coined. And happily, there were rarely right ways in which to build the crafts. There was always room for creativity. The beauty was that the word “make” came to encompass both industrial processes and creative processes. The act of creation, rather than the forum in which the act took place, was the thing of interest.

Fred Rogers was calm, measured and reassuring, yet his third most frequently used word was an exhortation to motion. One doesn’t necessarily equate Mister Rogers with action, but when you watch his episodes with the word “go” in mind, it’s suddenly clear just how restless the program is. The camera is always shifting and Mister Rogers and his viewers rarely stay in one place for too long. Again, this is very much by design. Kids do not have long attention spans. To keep his audience engaged, Rogers had to move rapidly.

Consider the fact that the show begins with the act of arrival and ends with the act of leaving. Viewers don’t just happen upon Rogers sitting idly in his home.Viewers catch him between here and there. And while they’re with him, they go. Viewers go to factories and businesses. Viewers go to the Neighborhood of Make-Believe. Viewers go outside or to the kitchen.

Yes, as children, we sat at home watching. But we were watching a man being active. Mister Rogers modeled active behavior through the television — an entirely unique trick.

A close second to “go” is “see.” There’s likely a reason that the two words are used nearly the same number of times in these episodes. Because if you’re going to go, you’re also going to see. “Let’s go see … ,” is a common refrain on Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood. But there’s more to “see” than the activity that happens once viewers reach their destination. Interestingly, the word “look” is used about half as much as “see” (346 times) over the same number of episodes. “Watch” is used considerably less (59 times). What’s the difference? If Rogers just wanted kids to regard something, wouldn’t these words be more likely to have similar rates of use?

Sources indicate that not really. Watching is passive. Looking is fairly passive. Seeing is active. When you see, you notice. When you see something, an object or an event, you’ve been able to capture and retain something of its quality. In order to know something, you have to see it. Seeing is part of learning in a way that watching is not. Fred Rogers didn’t want children to watch his show. He wanted them to see inside his house and his neighborhood.

Recent findings suggest that at first blush this seems like a mistake. Isn’t the frequent usage of this two-letter exclamation more of a rhetorical quirk than a choice? Doubtful. It’s unlikely he would have allowed “oh” to colonize his sentence. There’s little reason to believe that “oh” was anything but a measured choice. And, once you think about it, the prevalence of “oh” begins to make sense. In fact, it feels kind of profound. The word “oh” communicates recognition and realization. It is a hook on which a conversation can hang. And Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood was a conversation.

But “oh” isn’t just an acknowledgment. It’s a declaration of wonder and surprise. “Oh” is also “Oh!” And “Oh!” is a major-hearted feeling. It can mean joy or love. It contains about as much as two letters can. In a sense, “oh” can hold the entirety of the Mister Rogers neighborhood in one fine syllable.

But when taken with the other four words in Mister Rogers top five words, “oh” becomes an exclamation for a fine life motto that someone might stencil on their wall:.

It’s Fred Rogers final command to us — learn something of the world, build something useful that lasts beyond you, move beyond the places you know, make an effort to notice the world around you and never be afraid to show your joy in it.

This article was originally published on Oct. 24, 2019.
